These organizations also start with stricter organization settings. Featured connectors and skills, SSH hosts, Modal, model endpoints, and memory are off until you turn them on (including for members who were already using them), custom connectors and access to previously saved Claude Science work can't be turned on, and the organization always manages the network allowlist. See [Defaults by plan](/docs/claude-science/admin-controls#defaults-by-plan).

## Turn off Claude Science

Go to **Organization settings** > **Claude Science** and turn off the **Enable for your organization** toggle. Members can no longer sign in to the app, and members who are already signed in lose access within a few minutes. The app stops accepting new messages and shows a notice that Claude Science isn't available for their account. The other settings on the page keep their values and apply again when you turn Claude Science back on. Data already on members' computers stays there; see [How Claude Science works with your data](/docs/claude-science/how-claude-science-works-with-your-data) for details.

# Genetic drift in a bottle: Buri's 107 fruit-fly populations
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/bio-drift

Simulate 107 bottles of 16 fruit flies drifting by chance alone and compare them with Peter Buri's real bottles (1956).

![Three panels: 107 simulated allele-frequency paths over 19 generations, histograms at generations 1, 5, 10, and 19, and 20,000 replays at 16 and 9 breeding flies against Buri's 58.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/bio-drift-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=2e5d4d7b916e451a8f4d3fcdbcdb7dd9)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
In a 1956 paper, Peter Buri described keeping 107 bottles of fruit flies for 19 generations, restarting each bottle every generation with 8 males and 8 females picked at random. Every founder carried one copy each of two neutral eye-color alleles, bw and bw75, so bw75 started at a frequency of 0.5 in every bottle.

Simulate this with random sampling only: no selection, no mutation. Plot the bw75 frequency in all 107 populations over time, and draw histograms of the 107 frequencies at generations 1, 5, 10 and 19. Under each, print how many bottles are at 0, below 1/3, between 1/3 and 2/3, above 2/3, and at 1, and describe the change using only these 5 counts.

By generation 19, Buri found bw75 lost in 30 bottles and fixed in 28. Repeat your simulated experiment 1,000 times: how often does chance alone give that many? What population size would match his result? Compare it with Buri's own estimate for these bottles, about 9 breeding flies (2Ne = 17.86). Buri wrote that the causes are not known, but that unequal numbers of offspring per fly, down to sterility, are certainly part of it. This simulation does not test that, so report it as his view, in 1 or 2 sentences, and add no other causes. Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

107 simulated bottles of 16 fruit flies drift by chance alone: on average 25 lose or fix an allele in 19 generations (27 in the run pictured), but in Peter Buri's real bottles (1956) the count reached 58. A breeding population of about 9 gives 57, in line with Buri's own estimate (2Ne = 17.86): the textbook lesson of effective population size. Along the way the 107 frequencies, counted at generations 1, 5, 10, and 19, drain from the middle third into the outer thirds and from there into the 2 ends, 0 and 1, which no bottle leaves.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

Reference: Buri P., 'Gene frequency in small populations of mutant Drosophila', Evolution 10:367–402 (1956)


# A titration curve from the full equilibrium: which indicator finds the equivalence point?
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/chem-titration

Solve the full equilibrium for 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid as 0.100 M NaOH is added, without the usual shortcuts.

![Left: acetic acid's titration curve, with pH 2.88 at the start, 4.76 half-way, and 8.73 at equivalence. Right: acetic acid and HCl with the methyl orange and phenolphthalein ranges shaded: for acetic acid, methyl orange turns 17.4 mL too early.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/chem-titration-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=37e8dfb5f136ac8d3872d9cd328d04be)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
I'm titrating 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid (pKa 4.76) with 0.100 M NaOH. Compute the pH after each addition of base, from 0 to 50 mL, by solving the full equilibrium (mass balance, charge balance, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴) without the usual shortcuts (no Henderson–Hasselbalch, no 'x is small'), using concentrations, at 25 °C. Plot the titration curve and mark the starting point, the half-equivalence point and the equivalence point. Show that the acid alone sets the start, pH = pKa half-way, and acetate acting as a weak base sets the equivalence point.

Add the curve for 0.100 M HCl, and shade the color-change ranges of methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4) and phenolphthalein (pH 8.3–10.0). Give the pH of both curves at 24.95 and 25.05 mL to show how steep each jump is. Which indicator works for which acid? If I picked the wrong one, how far off would my endpoint be, in mL (endpoint = completed color change)? Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

With acetic acid, phenolphthalein turns within 0.05 mL of the 25.00 mL equivalence point; methyl orange has fully turned at 7.6 mL, 17.4 mL too early. Methyl orange works for HCl (0.02 mL early). The reason: from 24.95 to 25.05 mL the pH runs from 4.0 to 10.0 for HCl but from 7.5 to 10.0 for acetic acid, entirely above methyl orange's range. Solving the full equilibrium for 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid as 0.100 M NaOH is added, without the usual shortcuts, using concentrations, at 25 °C, gives pH 2.88 at the start, 4.76 = pKa at the half-way point, and 8.73 at the equivalence point.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.


# A first Kaplan–Meier curve: the 1963 leukemia trial of 6-MP
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/clin-km

Compare 6-MP against placebo with Kaplan–Meier curves from 42 remission times typed into the prompt.

![Two Kaplan–Meier plots: 6-MP and placebo remission curves with medians of 23 and 8 weeks (log-rank p = 0.00004), and the 6-MP curve three ways, with medians of 23, 16, and 10 weeks.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/clin-km-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=c4d20dad5701ebceb1d87c476424d2d3)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
In 1963 Freireich and colleagues published an early randomized, placebo-controlled trial of a chemotherapy drug: 42 patients under 20 with acute leukemia in remission got either 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) or a placebo, and were followed until they relapsed or the trial was stopped, which happened early, once 6-MP was clearly ahead. These are the weeks each patient stayed in remission. A + means the patient was still in remission when the trial was stopped.

6-MP: 6, 6, 6, 6+, 7, 9+, 10, 10+, 11+, 13, 16, 17+, 19+, 20+, 22, 23, 25+, 32+, 32+, 34+, 35+
Placebo: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 8, 8, 8, 8, 11, 11, 12, 12, 15, 17, 22, 23

Draw the Kaplan–Meier curve of each arm, with tick marks for the + patients and the numbers at risk under the plot. Give the median remission time in each arm and compare the arms with a log-rank test. Then show me what happens to the 6-MP median if I count every + as a relapse, or if I leave those patients out. Explain each step as you would to a medical student.
```

## Reference analysis

Median remission 23 weeks on 6-MP against 8 on placebo (log-rank p = 0.00004): Kaplan–Meier curves from 42 remission times typed into the prompt. Mishandling the 12 patients still in remission gives a 6-MP median of 16 or 10 weeks instead. The data are the 42 patients analyzed when the trial Freireich and colleagues published in 1963 was stopped; both medians and χ² = 16.79 match the textbook values.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

References:

* Freireich E.J. et al., 'The effect of 6-mercaptopurine on the duration of steroid-induced remissions in acute leukemia: a model for evaluation of other potentially useful therapy', Blood 21(6):699–716 (1963), doi:10.1182/blood.V21.6.699.699
* Kleinbaum D.G. & Klein M., Survival Analysis: A Self-Learning Text, 3rd ed.


# PageRank on a web of 11 pages: why 1 good link beats 6 weak ones
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/cs-pagerank-tiny

Follow a random surfer on Wikipedia's 11-page example until the numbers settle, and reproduce all 11 published values to 0.1 point.

![Three panels: the 11-page web as circles sized by PageRank, the 11 shares settling to B 38.4%, C 34.3%, and E 8.1%, and bars showing that C's one link brings 32.7 points while E's six bring 6.5.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/cs-pagerank-tiny-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=44bf56115d462e279420a8cfb04b1499)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
PageRank is the idea that launched Google (Brin & Page, 1998): a page matters if pages that matter link to it. Here is a tiny web of 11 pages, A to K, where B→C means that page B links to page C:

B→C, C→B, D→A, D→B, E→B, E→D, E→F, F→B, F→E, G→B, G→E, H→B, H→E, I→B, I→E, J→E, K→E

Imagine a surfer who follows a random link on the current page 85 % of the time and jumps to a random page the rest of the time. From a page with no links, the surfer always jumps to a random page. Start with the surfer equally likely to be on any page, and repeat that step until the share of time spent on each page stops changing. That share is the page's PageRank.

Draw the web as circles with area proportional to PageRank, each letter inside its circle, C and E in color, no other labels, and plot how the 11 numbers settle. This is the example drawn in Wikipedia's PageRank article; its values are B 38.4 %, C 34.3 %, E 8.1 %, D and F 3.9 %, A 3.3 %, G to K 1.6 %. Then compare each page's PageRank with its share of the 17 links. C has 1 incoming link, but it is B's only link, and ranks 2nd; E has 6, all from low-ranked pages, and gets 8.1 %. Show how many points each link brings to C and to E. Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

Page C has 1 incoming link and ranks 2nd (34.3%); page E has 6 and gets 8.1%. Follows a random surfer on Wikipedia's 11-page example until the numbers settle, and reproduces all 11 published values to 0.1 point (B 38.4%, C 34.3%, E 8.1%, …). C's link is B's only link and brings 32.7 points; E's 6 links come from low-ranked pages and bring 6.5 points together; every page also gets the same 1.6-point floor. Draws the web as circles with area proportional to PageRank and shows the 11 numbers settling: every page is within 0.1 point of its final value after 29 steps.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

Example web after [PageRanks-Example.svg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PageRanks-Example.svg) by 345Kai and Stannered (Wikimedia Commons, public domain).

Reference: S. Brin & L. Page, 'The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine', Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30, 107–117 (1998)


# A first finite-element model: a clamped steel ruler bends and vibrates
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/eng-beam

Split a 300 mm steel ruler clamped at one end into 4 beam elements and check its bending under 1 N and its first 3 vibration modes against beam theory.

![Three plots: the ruler bent under 1 N, tip 0.800 mm down as theory says; its first 3 mode shapes at 27.18, 170.53, and 480.62 Hz over theory; and frequency errors falling from 2 to 16 elements.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/eng-beam-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=f7c1012ed8af806d3ec445c6973cf630)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
I'm learning the finite-element method. Model a steel ruler clamped at one end: length 300 mm, width 25 mm, thickness 3 mm, E = 200 GPa, density 7850 kg/m³. Split it into 4 standard 2-node beam elements (cubic shape functions, consistent mass matrix) and write the matrices yourself with numpy. First hang 1 N (about 100 g) on the free end: beam theory says the tip drops PL³/(3EI) = 0.800 mm. Check that you get it, and draw the bent ruler over the theory curve. Then let the ruler vibrate: plot its first 3 mode shapes, each labeled with its frequency. Theory gives 27.18, 170.33 and 476.93 Hz; finite-element frequencies land slightly above and get closer with more elements, so show that in a small table for 2, 4, 8 and 16 elements. Give each frequency to 2 decimals, and its error in % worked out from the unrounded frequencies. Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

A 300 mm steel ruler clamped at one end is cut into 4 beam elements: under 1 N its tip drops 0.800 mm, exactly as beam theory says. Its first 3 vibration modes come out at 27.18, 170.53, and 480.62 Hz against 27.18, 170.33, and 476.93 Hz in theory, and 16 elements bring all 3 within 0.004%.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.


# A first X-ray diffraction pattern: why silicon shows 6 peaks and salt 9
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/mat-xrd

Simulate the X-ray powder patterns of silicon and table salt and label every peak with Bragg's law.

![Simulated X-ray diffraction patterns: silicon has 6 labeled peaks, with 200, 222, and 420 marked absent; rock salt has 9.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/mat-xrd-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=6d56de735b8fe6c1fd456f7259fc7d4d)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
X-ray diffraction is how we know where the atoms sit in a crystal. Simulate the powder diffraction patterns of silicon (diamond structure, a = 5.4311 Å) and rock salt (NaCl, a = 5.6402 Å) with pymatgen, for copper Kα₁ X-rays (wavelength="CuKa1", λ = 1.54056 Å) and angles 2θ up to 90°. Nothing needs downloading. Label every peak with its Miller indices hkl, and check each angle by hand with Bragg's law, λ = 2d sin θ, where d = a/√(h²+k²+l²). Both crystals share a face-centered cubic lattice, which allows 9 reflections in this range, yet silicon shows only 6: show that its 2-atom basis cancels 200, 222 and 420. In salt the all-odd peaks (111, 311, 331) are weak because Na and Cl scatter out of phase: show that too. Leave out other salts and what-ifs such as Na and Cl scattering equally, and round every number once, from its full-precision value. Put both patterns in 1 figure. Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

Simulates the X-ray powder patterns of silicon and table salt and labels every peak with Bragg's law. Both share a face-centered cubic lattice, yet below 2θ = 90° salt shows 9 peaks and silicon 6, because silicon's 2-atom basis cancels the 200, 222, and 420 reflections.

This example doesn't download any data.


# The Ulam spiral: are the primes' diagonal streaks real?
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/math-ulam

Compare the share of primes per diagonal on Ulam's 1963 spiral of 1 to 40,401 against as many random odd numbers.

![Primes up to 40,401 on Ulam's spiral, with primes of n² + n + 41 in orange along 2 rays; as many random odd numbers, with no streaks; and histograms of each diagonal's share, wider for the primes.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/math-ulam-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=140ca573e05d853818df9ab149c1f064)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
In 1963 the mathematician Stanisław Ulam, doodling during a long and boring talk, wrote the whole numbers in a square spiral and circled the primes. Recreate his picture. Find all primes up to 40,401 (= 201 × 201) with a sieve of Eratosthenes, and check that 1,229 of them are below 10,000. Write 1, 2, 3, … in a square spiral starting from the center, and mark the primes.

Are the diagonal streaks real, or is my eye fooling me? Draw the same picture with the same number of randomly chosen odd numbers. For every diagonal of odd numbers at least 100 cells long, in both directions, compute the share of marked cells, and compare its standard deviation and range in the 2 pictures.

Then highlight the numbers n² + n + 41 (Euler's polynomial). On this spiral about the first 40 values wind around the center, and from then on they run along 2 straight diagonals. How many of the first 100 are prime, and how many would you expect from typical odd numbers of that size? The first one that is not prime is n = 40, which gives 41 × 41. Which diagonals are rich in primes is predicted by a conjecture of Hardy and Littlewood (1923) that is still unproven: mention it, and describe the rich and poor diagonals without accounting for them. Walk me through your method at undergraduate level.
```

## Reference analysis

Yes. On Ulam's 1963 spiral of 1 to 40,401, the share of primes per diagonal runs from 0 to 48%, against roughly 11 to 32% for as many random odd numbers. Over the 202 diagonals of at least 100 cells that spread is about 2.3 times the random one, so the streaks are real. The sieve finds 4,236 primes, 1,229 of them below 10,000, as published. Euler's n² + n + 41 traces the 2 richest streaks (over 70% prime along its 2 rays, each one half of a diagonal, running outward from the diagonal's cell nearest the center): prime for n = 0 to 39, and for 86 of its first 100 values, where typical odd numbers of that size would give about 29 of 100.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

Reference: M. L. Stein, S. M. Ulam and M. B. Wells, 'A visual display of some properties of the distribution of primes', American Mathematical Monthly 71, 516–520 (1964)


# The double slit, one electron at a time
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/phys-doubleslit

Rebuild the picture of Tonomura's 1989 experiment with an ideal double slit: each electron lands as 1 random dot, yet fringes 10.7 µm apart build up.

![Dots after 10 to 100,000 electrons build up into fringes; a histogram fit gives a spacing of 10.706 ± 0.003 µm against λL/d = 10.711 µm, and a smooth curve shows no fringes when the slit is known.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/phys-doubleslit-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=d33485dbb10e2b0e60ce7127967ae21c)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
In 1989 Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi sent electrons one at a time past an electron biprism, the electron version of a double slit, and filmed an interference pattern building up dot by dot. Recreate that with an ideal double slit. Say nothing else about the 1989 experiment.

Take electrons accelerated through 50 kV (work out their de Broglie wavelength, with relativity), 2 slits 0.1 µm wide and 0.5 µm apart, and a screen 1 m away (check that d²/λL ≈ 0.05, so the simple far-field formula holds). Compute the probability of landing at each position on the screen. Then draw random hits from it, one electron at a time, and show the screen from −60 to 60 µm after 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 electrons, noting on the figure how many hits land outside.

Fit the final pattern to measure the fringe spacing, and give it with its error bar: how many error bars from λL/d? Then show that the fringes vanish if we know which slit each electron went through. Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

Each electron lands as 1 random dot, yet fringes 10.7 µm apart build up. Rebuilds the picture of Tonomura's 1989 experiment with an ideal double slit: 50 kV electrons (de Broglie wavelength 5.355 pm, 2.4% shorter than without relativity), 2 slits 0.1 µm wide and 0.5 µm apart, a screen at 1 m. 10 electrons look random, 100 hint at bands, by 1,000 the fringes are plain, and at 100,000 a fit gives 10.71 µm, good to about 0.003 µm, matching λL/d = 10.711 µm. If we know which slit each electron went through, the fringes vanish and only the broad single-slit envelope is left.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

Reference: A. Tonomura, J. Endo, T. Matsuda, T. Kawasaki & H. Ezawa, 'Demonstration of single-electron buildup of an interference pattern', American Journal of Physics 57, 117–120 (1989)


# Schelling's segregation model: ask for 30% same-color neighbors, end up with 75%
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/example-gallery/soc-schelling-small

Ask for 30% same-color neighbors, end up with about 75%: the textbook computer version of Thomas Schelling's 1971 idea.

![A random board of blue and orange households (49% of neighbors alike), the same board settled into one-color patches (75%), and a curve of the share alike at the end against the demand, 51.3% to 99.6%.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-ai/F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI/images/claude-science/example-gallery/soc-schelling-small-full-light.webp?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=F2QP9ubtYgT0edFI\&q=85\&s=9150fb06019e6cb83311d70c1493c396)

The numbers in your session might differ from this picture and from the summary in [Reference analysis](#reference-analysis).

## Prompt

Copy the prompt and paste it into a new session in [Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/overview). By default, Claude asks with a [permission card](/docs/claude-science/core-concepts#permission-cards) before it runs code or installs packages.

```text Prompt wrap theme={null}
In 1971 the economist Thomas Schelling showed, with chips on a checkerboard, that a city can segregate sharply even when nobody asks for more than an even mix. Recreate the textbook computer version, which segregates at even milder demands. Fill a 50 × 50 grid at random with 1,125 blue and 1,125 orange households, leaving 250 cells empty. A household is content if at least 30 % of its occupied neighboring cells (the 8 around it, fewer at the edges) hold its own color. With 8 occupied neighbors, that means at least 3 of its own color, so it accepts 5 of the other. Each discontent household moves to a random empty cell; repeat until everyone is content. Show the grid before and after and measure the average share of like-colored neighbors: it starts near 50 %. Where does it end? How many points is that above the random board, and how many above the 30 % they asked for?

Then replace the 30 % by 10 %, 20 %, up to 70 % and plot what households get against what they ask for. Judge each result against the random board's 50 %, not against the demand: 10 % and 20 % stay within 10 points of it, the largest jump (about 18 points) is from 20 % to 30 %, and separation is nearly total from 60 %. Allow 500 rounds. Title each figure with what it shows. Give changes between thresholds in percentage points rather than in words like "half" or "triple". Explain each step as you would to an undergraduate.
```

## Reference analysis

Ask for 30% same-color neighbors, end up with about 75%. On a 50 × 50 grid filled at random with 1,125 blue and 1,125 orange households and 250 empty cells (about 50% of neighbors alike), only about 18% of households are discontent. Yet once each discontent one has moved to a random empty cell (roughly 1,000 moves in 10 to 20 rounds), the board is a patchwork of 1-color neighborhoods. Redone for demands of 10% to 70%, 20 random boards each: 10% leaves the random board as it is (51%), 20% lifts it to 57%, 50% gives 88% (about 7 like neighbors for each unlike one), and separation is nearly total from 60% (98% at 60%, 99.6% at 70%). The textbook computer version of Thomas Schelling's 1971 idea.

## Data

This example doesn't download any data.

Reference: T. C. Schelling, 'Dynamic models of segregation', Journal of Mathematical Sociology 1(2), 143–186 (1971)


# Get started
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/get-started

Install Claude Science on macOS, Windows, or Linux, sign in with your Claude account, and run your first analysis.

Install Claude Science on your computer, sign in with your Claude account, and run your first analysis. You need a Claude Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise plan. The [Claude Team plan for scientists](https://claude.com/programs/team-plan-for-scientists) has Claude Science on by default. On other Team and Enterprise plans, an Owner must [turn Claude Science on](/docs/claude-science/enable-claude-science) first. For what each plan includes and how usage works, see [Plans and usage](/docs/claude-science/overview#plans-and-usage).

## Install

> [tab] macOS
>
> Download the installer from [claude.com/product/claude-science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) and double-click to install. On first launch, the app sets up its runtime and starter Python and R environments, which takes a few minutes, then opens a new tab in your default browser. If no browser tab appears, click **Claude Science** in the Dock.
>
> **Updates.** Installing an update from inside Claude Science can switch it from a browser tab to its own window. See [Claude Science in its own window on macOS](/docs/claude-science/mac-app-window).
>
> * **If it opens in a browser tab**: Claude Science checks for updates in the background and shows **Update available** when one is ready. Choose **Restart to update** to install it.
> * **If it opens in its own window**: Claude Science downloads updates by itself and installs them when you quit. To check for an update right away, choose **Claude Science > Check for App Updates…** in the menu bar.

> [tab] Windows
>
> Download the installer from [claude.com/product/claude-science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) and open it. It installs Claude Science for your user account, adds **Claude Science** to the Start menu and the desktop, and opens the app in its own window. The installer is signed by Anthropic, PBC. On first launch, Claude Science sets up the sandbox and downloads its app window engine (about 150 MB) from `downloads.claude.ai` before the window appears, so the first start takes longer than later ones, and a notice shows progress. The starter Python and R environments keep setting up in the background for several minutes after the window opens.
>
> **One-time Windows permission.** If Claude Science asks for one-time permission from Windows so that cells can run git and Command Prompt scripts and PowerShell can change folders, **Yes** lets Windows ask for approval (an administrator's password if you aren't one) and **No** leaves those features off. Python and R cells work either way, and the **Ask Windows now** button under **Settings** > **Permissions** grants the permission later.
>
> **Notification-area icon.** Closing the window leaves Claude Science running, with an icon in the notification area of the taskbar. Click the icon to reopen the window, or choose **Quit Claude Science** from the icon's menu to stop the app.
>
> **Updates.** Claude Science checks for updates in the background and shows **Update available** when one is ready; choose **Restart to update** to install it. Administrators who distribute the app themselves can turn the background check off with `auto_update = false` under `[update]` in `config.toml` (see [Manage Claude Science on devices](/docs/claude-science/manage-on-devices#deploy-configuration-with-device-management)). To update Claude Science yourself instead, open a newer installer, which upgrades the installed copy in place and keeps your data.
>
> **Uninstall.** To remove the app, follow the Windows steps in [Uninstall Claude Science](#uninstall-claude-science).
>
> **Corporate networks.** Claude Science follows the proxy configured in Windows proxy settings and trusts corporate root certificates installed for the whole computer, so most managed PCs need no Claude Science configuration. See [Use Claude Science on a corporate network](/docs/claude-science/corporate-networks).
>
> **Differences on Windows:**
>
> * Claude runs shell commands with PowerShell. Command Prompt scripts, git inside cells, and folder changes in PowerShell need the one-time Windows permission.
> * Only folders on local NTFS or ReFS drives can be granted, not network shares, mapped network drives, FAT or exFAT drives (many USB sticks and memory cards), or a whole drive such as `D:\`. Copy such files to a local folder or attach them in the chat.
> * [Custom connectors](/docs/claude-science/custom-connectors) that run a local command start with `npx`, `node`, `python`, or the full path of a program. Connectors launched through `npm` or a `.cmd`, `.bat`, or `.ps1` file aren't supported.
> * The **Model endpoints** section of **Settings** > **Compute** (NVIDIA BioNeMo NIM) isn't available.
>
> **Linux version under WSL.** To use Claude Science from a Linux environment on your Windows computer, run the Linux command-line version under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL 2, not WSL 1) with Ubuntu 24.04 or later. The Windows app itself doesn't need WSL. Inside the Ubuntu terminal, follow the install steps in the Linux tab, then start Claude Science with `claude-science serve --port 8765 --no-browser` and open the printed link, which starts with `http://127.0.0.1:8765`, in a Windows browser. Projects you create there stay in WSL, and the Windows app keeps its own.
>
> If Claude Science under WSL shows one of these errors or problems, use the matching fix:
>
> * `daemon already running`: Claude Science is already running. Run `claude-science url` to print a fresh link, and open it in a Windows browser.
> * `port 8765 is already in use`: another program, or another copy of Claude Science, has that port. Start with a different one, for example `--port 8080`.
> * The link stops working: check that Claude Science is still running with `claude-science status`. If it's still running, run `claude-science url` for a fresh link and open it in a Windows browser. Claude Science stops when WSL shuts down, for example after `wsl --shutdown`. Start it again by running `claude-science serve --port 8765 --no-browser` in the Ubuntu terminal.
> * An SSH host can't be added: under WSL, Claude Science reads the SSH settings in Ubuntu's `~/.ssh`, not the ones in Windows. Copy the host's entry from `C:\Users\<you>\.ssh\config`, and its key file, into Ubuntu's `~/.ssh` folder, then run `chmod 600` on them.
> * `The database is on /mnt/*`: Claude Science's data folder is on a Windows drive, which it can't use under WSL. Move the folder into your Ubuntu home folder, such as the default `~/.claude-science`, and if you set `data_dir` or `--data-dir`, point it there. If you use a folder other than the default, choose a new, empty one, because Claude Science can delete files in that folder that it didn't create.

> [tab] Linux
>
> Install the sandbox dependencies, then run the installer. The sandbox needs bubblewrap 0.8.0 or later and socat, and installing them for the whole system takes administrator (root or `sudo`) access. Claude Science runs them from system folders such as `/usr/bin` and `/usr/local/bin` and doesn't search your PATH. If you don't have administrator access, ask your system administrator to install them, or [approve a copy of your own](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server#approve-your-own-copy-of-bubblewrap-or-socat), such as one from conda.
>
> * Ubuntu or Debian: `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y curl bubblewrap socat`
> * Fedora or RHEL: `sudo dnf install -y curl bubblewrap socat`
> * Arch: `sudo pacman -S curl bubblewrap socat`
>
> Ubuntu 24.04's repositories carry a new enough bubblewrap and Ubuntu 22.04's don't; on any distribution, confirm with `/usr/bin/bwrap --version` that the installed version is 0.8.0 or later before you start Claude Science.
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install-claude-science.sh | bash
> ```
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> claude-science serve
> ```
>
> First launch prints a local URL right away, then continues setting up its starter Python and R environments. To run Claude Science on a remote server and use it from your computer, see [Run on a remote Linux server](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server).

To update Claude Science later, or when it asks you to update, see [Update Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/update-claude-science).

> [!NOTE]
>
> Claude Science is a local application, not a website, so there's no public URL to visit. On Windows it opens in its own window, and on Linux it opens in a browser tab. On a Mac it opens in a browser tab, or in its own window once an update has switched it over (see [Claude Science in its own window on macOS](/docs/claude-science/mac-app-window)). Open it from the application itself: Claude Science in Applications or the Dock on macOS, the Start menu on Windows, or the `claude-science` command on Linux. On a remote server, the sign-in link reaches your browser through an SSH tunnel; see [Run on a remote Linux server](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server).

## Sign in and complete setup

When the app opens, sign in with your Claude account. If Claude Science opens in its own window, on Windows or on a Mac, click the **Sign in on the web** button and confirm with **Continue**. Claude Science then opens claude.ai in your default browser. Once you approve the sign-in there, Claude Science continues in its own window. No API key is required.

In a browser tab or in the Windows app, if you approve the sign-in in your browser but Claude Science doesn't continue (for example, on a remote server when the sign-in can't return through the SSH tunnel), sign in with a code instead:

1. Go back to the Claude Science sign-in screen and select **Paste code instead**, then **Open on web**.
2. Approve access in the browser, then copy the whole code the page shows.
3. Paste the code into Claude Science. If the sign-in doesn't continue on its own, select **Continue**.

After sign-in, a setup wizard walks you through enabling connectors and skills, setting which websites Claude can access, and choosing whether memory is on. You can change these at any time in Settings.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Claude Science keeps your data in a single folder in your home directory: `~/.claude-science` on macOS and Linux, and `%USERPROFILE%\.claude-science` on Windows. On Linux, the `claude-science` command itself installs to `~/.local/bin`, and on Windows the app installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ClaudeScience` and adds that folder to your user PATH. Beyond that, it doesn't modify your existing conda installation, R libraries, or shell configuration. To remove Claude Science, see [Uninstall Claude Science](#uninstall-claude-science).

## Run your first analysis

* Open the Example project, or create a new one.
* Start a conversation. Reference a folder on your computer by typing its path or using the @ picker in the composer.
* Review the folder-access card when it appears and choose whether to allow it.
* Review the code-execution card when Claude proposes running code and choose whether to allow it.
* Results appear as artifacts in the Files panel.

## Uninstall Claude Science

Uninstalling removes the application and keeps your data folder. Your projects, artifacts, and conversation history stay on your computer until you delete that folder.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Deleting the data folder (`~/.claude-science`, or `%USERPROFILE%\.claude-science` on Windows) removes all your projects, artifacts, conversation history, environments, and settings, and signs you out. Copy anything you want to keep first, with **Download** on an artifact or by copying the project's folder from inside the data folder.
>
> Before you uninstall, check where your data is under **Settings > Storage > Data location**. If it shows a folder other than the default, the default folder still holds your environments and your sign-in, and it can also hold projects from before that location was set. To remove all your data:
>
> * The folder that **Data location** shows holds your current projects. Move anything else you stored there yourself out of it, then delete that folder.
> * Delete the default folder (`~/.claude-science`, or `%USERPROFILE%\.claude-science` on Windows).
>
> Files in the folders you granted Claude access to aren't affected unless they're inside the folder that **Data location** shows.

> [tab] macOS
>
> **1. Quit Claude Science**
>
> In the Dock, Control-click the **Claude Science** icon and choose **Quit**. If you started Claude Science from Terminal with `claude-science serve`, also run `claude-science stop`.
>
> **2. Move the application to the Trash**
>
> In Finder, open the **Applications** folder and move **Claude Science** to the Trash. If **Claude Science** isn't there, look in the **Applications** folder inside your home folder.
>
> **3. Remove the Terminal command**
>
> The app also adds a `claude-science` command for Terminal. Remove it with `rm ~/.local/bin/claude-science`.
>
> To remove your data as well, delete the `~/.claude-science` folder. If Claude Science opened in its own window, also delete `~/Library/Application Support/Claude Science`, which holds that window's own settings and stored data.

> [tab] Windows
>
> **1. Quit Claude Science**
>
> Right-click the Claude Science icon in the notification area of the taskbar and choose **Quit Claude Science**. The uninstaller doesn't run while the app is running.
>
> **2. Uninstall the app**
>
> In Windows **Settings**, go to **Apps > Installed apps** and uninstall **Claude Science**, or run `claude-science uninstall` in a terminal.
>
> To remove the app and your data together, use `claude-science uninstall --purge` instead. It deletes the whole folder your data location points to, including anything you stored there yourself, so move those files out first.
>
> When your data location isn't `%USERPROFILE%\.claude-science`, `--purge` leaves that folder in place. It still holds your environments and your sign-in, and it can also hold projects from before that location was set. To remove those too, delete `%USERPROFILE%\.claude-science` yourself.

> [tab] Linux
>
> For the Linux version under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), run these commands in the Ubuntu terminal.
>
> **1. Stop Claude Science**
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> claude-science stop
> ```
>
> **2. Delete the command**
>
> ```bash theme={null}
> rm ~/.local/bin/claude-science
> ```
>
> If you installed it somewhere else, `command -v claude-science` shows where.
>
> To remove your data as well, delete the `~/.claude-science` folder.

To reinstall, follow [Install](#install) again. Installing doesn't replace an existing data folder.

## Troubleshooting first launch

* macOS says the application isn't supported, or the app icon appears crossed out: the download page picked the build for the wrong processor. Return to the download page and choose Mac (Intel) or Mac (Apple Silicon) to match your Mac. To check which you have, open the Apple menu, choose About This Mac, and look at the Chip or Processor line.
* Nothing opened on macOS, or no browser tab appeared on Linux: on macOS, click **Claude Science** in the Dock, or open it from the **Applications** folder. On Linux, copy the printed URL into a browser on the same machine, or run `claude-science url` to print a fresh one.
* On macOS, some of Claude's tools can't start and the error mentions the Xcode license, usually right after an Xcode update: macOS won't run the Python that comes with Apple's developer tools until the license is accepted. Open Xcode and agree to the license with an administrator account, or run `sudo xcodebuild -license accept` in Terminal, then ask Claude to try again.
* A Claude Science message on Windows says the app was not installed because the file could not be confirmed: the copy you opened still runs but isn't installed. Download the installer again from [claude.com/product/claude-science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) and open the new file. If the message persists, the PC could not verify the publisher's signature, so ask your IT team.
* The Windows app reports that it couldn't set up the app window engine: the first launch downloads that engine from `downloads.claude.ai`, and this usually means the app couldn't reach it. Check the internet connection, and on a corporate network ask IT to allow that domain (see [Network requirements](/docs/claude-science/network-requirements)).
* On Linux, the installer stops with `The download service may be unreachable, or not yet available in your region`: the installer couldn't get the latest version from `storage.googleapis.com`. Check the internet connection, and on a corporate network ask IT to allow that domain (see [Network requirements](/docs/claude-science/network-requirements#app-connections)). Claude Science is available where Anthropic offers claude.ai. See [Supported countries and regions](https://www.anthropic.com/supported-countries).
* On Linux, the installer stops with `was NOT installed` and says the copy you already had `was left as it is`: Claude Science was already installed, so the installer first tried to check that the new version starts on this computer. The check didn't succeed, so nothing was replaced. The message and the lines under it say why and, where there is a fix, what to do. If they point to the [configuration file](/docs/claude-science/configuration-file-reference), `~/.claude-science/config.toml`, fix what they report in that file, then run the installer again from the Linux tab of [Install](#install). If they give no fix, keep using the copy you already had.
* On Linux, the shell reports `command not found` for `claude-science`: `~/.local/bin` isn't on your PATH. Add the PATH line that the installer printed to your shell profile, then open a new terminal.
* On Linux, `claude-science serve` stops with a `Sandbox unavailable:` message that says `bwrap not found in` a list of folders, or `bwrap was found on PATH at` a path: bubblewrap isn't installed in a system folder. In version 0.1.71 and later, Claude Science runs bubblewrap and socat only from the system folders that the message lists or from a copy you've approved. It doesn't search your PATH. Install both with the command for your distribution in the Linux tab of [Install](#install). Without administrator access, [approve a copy of your own](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server#approve-your-own-copy-of-bubblewrap-or-socat) with the `claude-science sandbox approve` command that the message prints. If this happened after you typed `claude-science update`, you can [go back to version 0.1.70](/docs/claude-science/troubleshooting#not-approved).
* On Linux, `claude-science serve` stops with a `Sandbox unavailable:` message such as `/usr/bin/bwrap is too old`: the bubblewrap it names is older than 0.8.0. Check its version in a terminal with that path, for example `/usr/bin/bwrap --version`, then upgrade bubblewrap. Ubuntu 24.04's repositories carry a new enough version and Ubuntu 22.04's don't. If you can't upgrade it, [approve a newer copy of your own](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server#approve-your-own-copy-of-bubblewrap-or-socat).
* On Linux, `claude-science serve` stops with `Sandbox unavailable: bwrap cannot create unprivileged user namespaces`: the kernel or an AppArmor profile blocks the sandbox from creating user namespaces. The rest of the message names the settings to check on Ubuntu, Debian, and other distributions, and changing them takes administrator (`sudo`) access.
* On Linux, `claude-science serve` stops with `Sandbox unavailable: socat is required for Linux sandbox networking`: socat isn't installed in a system folder, and Claude Science doesn't search your PATH for it. Install socat with the command for your distribution in the Linux tab of [Install](#install). Without administrator access, you can [approve a copy of your own](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server#approve-your-own-copy-of-bubblewrap-or-socat) so that Claude Science starts. Until socat is in a system folder, environment setup fails with `Package downloads are being blocked by network policy`, because code that Claude runs has no network access. If this happened after you typed `claude-science update`, you can [go back to version 0.1.70](/docs/claude-science/troubleshooting#not-approved).
* On Linux, a line starting `[sandbox]` says `sandboxed commands run without network access`, in the terminal where `claude-science serve` runs or in the output of `claude-science logs`: Claude Science started, but the sandbox has no network access. The sandbox runs socat only from system folders such as `/usr/bin`, and doesn't use a copy from conda, pixi, a cluster module, or your home folder, including a copy that you approved. Code that Claude runs can't reach the internet, and environment setup fails with `Package downloads are being blocked by network policy` even when your network blocks nothing. Install socat with the command for your distribution in the Linux tab of [Install](#install), or if you don't have administrator access, ask your system administrator to install it for the whole system.
* Projects from another computer don't appear: by design, Claude Science keeps your work on the computer where it's installed, so each computer starts with its own projects. Your earlier projects are still on the other computer. See [Use Claude Science on more than one computer](/docs/claude-science/multiple-computers).
* Projects you created under another sign-in on this computer don't appear automatically, for example, after you move from a personal plan to your organization's Team plan: your earlier projects are still in that sign-in's folder. Select the **Review** button on the banner at the top of the home screen, or select **Review** next to **Access previously saved Claude Science work on this computer** under **Settings** > **General** > **Account**, to access them. On Team and Enterprise plans, if there's no banner and the setting is grayed out, your admin controls it. See [Access work from another sign-in on your computer](/docs/claude-science/multiple-computers#access-work-from-another-sign-in-on-your-computer).
* Sign-in stops at claude.ai: your account is on the Free plan (upgrade required), the redirect couldn't return (in a browser tab or in the Windows app, use **Paste code instead**), or your Team or Enterprise organization hasn't [enabled Claude Science](/docs/claude-science/enable-claude-science) yet.
* After you paste a code, Claude Science says the code wasn't recognized or was issued for an earlier sign-in attempt: select **Open on web** again, approve access, and paste the whole new code. If it says `PKCE state missing or expired` instead, select **Back** and follow the steps in [Sign in and complete setup](#sign-in-and-complete-setup) again.


# Glossary
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/glossary

One-sentence definitions for the terms you meet in Claude Science, from artifact to workspace.

One-sentence definitions for the terms you meet in Claude Science, from artifact to workspace.

**[Artifact](/docs/claude-science/artifacts)**: any file Claude makes and saves for you, listed in its session's Files view.

**Cell**: one block of code Claude runs in a kernel; the cell, its output, and the environment it ran in are recorded in the session's Notebook.

**Cloud provider**: your own account at a cloud service where Claude can start jobs; you pay that provider directly.

**[Comment](/docs/claude-science/comments)**: a note you pin to part of an artifact by selecting it; Claude reads pending comments as instructions on its next turn.

**Connector**: an outside data source or tool wired into Claude over MCP; Claude Science includes a featured set, you can access partner connectors from the Connectors Directory, and you can add your own under Settings > Connectors.

**Data directory**: the `~/.claude-science` folder on your computer holding the database, artifacts, session workspaces, and logs.

**[Environment](/docs/claude-science/tools-and-environments)**: a named set of installed packages (conda) that a kernel runs in, reused across sessions.

**Execution log**: the slice of a session's Notebook cells that produced a given artifact version, shown as a tab in its Provenance pane.

**Kernel**: the live Python or R process that runs a session's cells and keeps variables in memory between them.

**Memory**: notes Claude keeps about you and your projects across sessions, which you can review and edit.

**Model endpoint**: a scientific domain-specific model server you register under Settings > Compute, that runs locally or connects to a vendor's hosted solution, that Claude sends single prediction requests to.

**Network allowlist**: the list of every outside host that sandboxed code may reach, kept under Settings or, on Team and Enterprise plans, managed by your organization.

**Permission card**: the card that replaces the message box when Claude needs your permission for running code, running a job, accessing a network host, a folder, a connector tool, a saved credential, or re-configuring Claude Science; you allow or deny it.

**Provenance (the artifact record)**: the panel behind every artifact version showing the code, cells, conversation, environment, and findings that produced it.

**[Reviewer](/docs/claude-science/the-reviewer)**: the independent agent that re-examines Claude's claims and artifacts at checkpoints, recording each issue it raises as a finding on the artifact's Review tab; on some plans it runs in the background automatically.

**Sandbox**: the isolated environment all of Claude's code runs in; reaching outside it needs your approval.

**Scope**: how long an approval lasts (Once, This conversation, This project, or Global), with every standing grant listed and revocable under Settings > Permissions.

**Session**: one conversation thread inside a project, with its own kernel and workspace.

**Skill**: an installable package of instructions and helper code that teaches Claude a method or tool.

**Specialist**: a named set of skills, connectors, and instructions that a session answers as.

**SSH host**: a remote machine (server, cluster node, or a job submission host) added by its SSH name, that Claude can run jobs on, or dispatch jobs from.

**[Use case](/docs/claude-science/safeguards#choose-a-use-case)**: a research purpose that Anthropic has approved for your organization under the Life Sciences Verification Program (beta); if you have more than one, you choose which one a session uses.

**Version**: one immutable save of an artifact; saving again adds a new version on top instead of overwriting.

**Workspace**: the per-session folder on disk where Claude's code reads and writes files before they are saved as artifacts.


# How Claude Science works with your data
Source: https://claude.com/docs/claude-science/how-claude-science-works-with-your-data

What Claude Science keeps on your computers, what it sends to Anthropic and how long Anthropic keeps it, who can access it, Anthropic's no-training and ownership commitments, and the controls available to your organization.

Claude Science is client-side software that your organization installs and runs on computers it controls, and Anthropic provides the Claude models the app calls. This page covers what that means for your research data.

## Model training and ownership of your work

On Team and Enterprise plans the [Commercial Terms of Service](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms) apply. Under them Anthropic "may not train models on Customer Content from Services," and, as between the parties and to the extent permitted by applicable law, your organization "retains all rights to its Inputs" and "owns its Outputs," including the analyses, code, and results your researchers produce with Claude Science. Anthropic may use content to improve its models only when your organization otherwise expressly chooses to allow it (see [Is my data used for model training?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training)). Safety feedback a member sends when Claude's safeguards pause a chat goes to Anthropic for future improvements to its safety systems. To turn off the ability for your researchers to provide feedback, an Owner can turn off the **Rate chats** toggle under **Organization settings** > **Data and privacy**.

On Pro and Max plans the [Consumer Terms of Service](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/consumer-terms), [Anthropic Privacy Policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/privacy), and your Claude privacy settings in the Settings panel apply (see [Legal and compliance](/docs/claude-science/legal-and-compliance)).

## Where Claude Science data lives

| Where | What |
| - | - |
| The computer running Claude Science | Conversation history, project files and artifacts, saved memory, most settings, and stored credentials, in a local folder Anthropic doesn't host or sync (see [Manage Claude Science on devices](/docs/claude-science/manage-on-devices)) |
| Anthropic | The items listed under [What Anthropic receives](#what-anthropic-receives) |
| Services your organization or members connect | Jobs, files, and queries sent to your SSH hosts, your Modal account, scientific model endpoints, cloud storage, and the external services that local (Featured and custom) connectors, sandboxed code, and remote jobs call, directly from the computer or your own compute and without passing through Anthropic (see [Admin controls](/docs/claude-science/admin-controls#organization-settings)) |

Sign-in tokens and the credentials members store for compute and cloud storage are encrypted on the computer, and the rest of the local folder relies on operating-system permissions, so apply your full-disk encryption and device management policies to it.

## What Anthropic receives

The app sends the following to Anthropic, over TLS and signed in with the member's Claude account (see [Network requirements](/docs/claude-science/network-requirements#app-connections) for the domains):

* **Requests to Claude** every time Claude responds, carrying the conversation so far, including the member's prompts, the contents of files Claude has read (PDFs included), code and command output, connector results, images Claude is shown, and recalled memory facts. Anthropic keeps these as model-call logs (see [What Anthropic keeps and for how long](#what-anthropic-keeps-and-for-how-long)).
* **Web search queries**, run by Anthropic's web search service through a third-party search provider listed among [Anthropic's subprocessors](https://www.anthropic.com/subprocessors).
* **Dictation audio**, streamed to Anthropic's speech-to-text service only while a member dictates. If the app can't use that service while Claude Science is open in a browser such as Chrome or Edge, it falls back to the browser's built-in speech recognition, and that browser's vendor then processes the audio.
* **Safety feedback**, only when a member sends it from the [**Chat paused** card](/docs/claude-science/safeguards#when-safeguards-flag-a-message) that appears when Claude's safeguards pause a chat, consisting of the member's optional comment and a copy of that conversation (members are reminded before submission) with known credential formats and email addresses redacted. It goes to Anthropic for future improvements to its safety systems. Not accepted from organizations with HIPAA compliance or customer-managed encryption keys.
* **Custom skills a member publishes**, stored with the member's claude.ai skills.
* **Usage telemetry and error reports**, which carry app, device, and timing data, plus account and organization identifiers on telemetry events, but no conversation content, file contents, or file names (see [Telemetry](/docs/claude-science/manage-on-devices#telemetry) for the device setting that turns them, and feedback, off).
* **Calls to connectors Anthropic hosts** from your claude.ai connector directory, which pass through Anthropic's connector service as in claude.ai, plus routine account, settings, and update traffic.

## What Anthropic keeps and for how long

For Team and Enterprise organizations, Anthropic processes this data under the [Data Processing Addendum](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/data-processing-addendum), encrypted at rest and in transit. Model-call logs follow Anthropic's [commercial data retention policy](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996866-how-long-do-you-store-my-organization-s-data), including its longer retention for content flagged by automated trust and safety systems or required by law.

Requests to models designated [Covered Models](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15425695-covered-models) are retained for 30 days to support Anthropic's safety work, as [Data retention practices for Covered Models](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15425996-data-retention-practices-for-covered-models) describes. Feedback submissions are kept under the feedback terms in the same policy.

## Who at Anthropic can access retained content

Human review of model-call logs, published skills, or Compliance API transcripts requires a specific reason, such as reviewing content that automated safety systems flagged, responding to a security incident, or meeting a legal obligation, through a controlled path where access is restricted to personnel whose role requires it and logged as the [Data Processing Addendum](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/data-processing-addendum) describes, and content reviewed this way isn't used to train Claude models. Feedback a member chooses to send is handled separately, as [Model training and ownership of your work](#model-training-and-ownership-of-your-work) describes. [Access Transparency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/access-transparency) records don't cover the Claude apps, including Claude Science.

## Controls available to your organization

* **Organization settings** for connectors, skills, the sandbox network allowlist, SSH hosts, Modal, model endpoints, memory, and access to previously saved Claude Science work (see [Admin controls](/docs/claude-science/admin-controls)). There is no organization setting for web search, dictation, or telemetry.
* **US-only inference** (usage-based Enterprise plans) runs model inference for Claude Science requests in the United States, as for your other Claude apps (see [Enable US-only inference](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15422948-enable-us-only-inference-for-your-organization)).
* **Device configuration** turns off telemetry, error reports, and feedback and relocates the local data folder (see [Manage Claude Science on devices](/docs/claude-science/manage-on-devices)).
* **Running Claude Science next to your data**, on a Linux server or virtual machine you control, keeps datasets on your infrastructure, apart from what Claude reads into the conversation, while Claude's inference runs on Anthropic's service (see [Run on a remote Linux server](/docs/claude-science/run-on-remote-linux-server)).
* **Usage analytics** show adoption and session metrics without conversation content (see [Monitor usage](/docs/claude-science/monitor-usage)).

## Compliance API coverage

On Enterprise plans with the [Compliance API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-api) enabled, your organization gets a record of Claude Science settings changes and its own read-only transcripts of members' Claude Science sessions (coverage is in beta), which are kept for your organization's own retention period (6 years by default) and, in organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, encrypted under your key. [Retrieve session transcripts](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-sessions) describes what a transcript contains and which sessions aren't captured, including those in organizations with HIPAA compliance enabled.

## Customer-managed encryption keys

Organizations that use [customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/cmek) can turn on Claude Science. The content Anthropic stores from the app is encrypted under your key, including the model-call logs of members' conversations with Claude, skills members publish, and, for Enterprise organizations with the Compliance API enabled, session transcripts.

The app's conversation history, files, artifacts, and memory are stored on the member's computer and aren't hosted by Anthropic; of these, only what the app sends to Claude reaches Anthropic, where your key covers it as this section describes. Work members send to their own SSH hosts, Modal account, or scientific model endpoints goes directly there, not through Anthropic, and isn't under your key or any Anthropic-managed key, so review those providers' data handling. You can turn these connections off under **Organization settings** > **Claude Science**.

In organizations with CMEK enabled, the app hides the **Send feedback** link on the [**Chat paused**](/docs/claude-science/safeguards#when-safeguards-flag-a-message) card.

## What isn't available for Claude Science

Zero data retention (a Claude Code zero-data-retention arrangement covers Claude Code sessions, not Claude Science), Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, coverage under Anthropic's Business Associate Agreement (keep protected health information out of Claude Science), and inference through a third-party cloud platform or your own cloud tenancy aren't available for Claude Science. See [Admin controls](/docs/claude-science/admin-controls#how-other-admin-settings-apply-to-claude-science) for how the other claude.ai admin settings apply to the app.
