Serve the script over `https://`.
* **Failed downloads.** The download can fail when the sandbox starts, for example right after a VPN change. For the address in the OS proxy settings, the app retries for about a minute and then again when new commands start in the sandbox. When a retry succeeds, commands that start afterward use the script without an app restart. A failed download leaves in place a script the shell already has from the same address. A response that isn't a PAC script, such as a sign-in page, counts as a failed download.
* **Host names with no dot.** Inside the sandbox, a host name with no dot in it is looked up under the device's DNS search domains when the name alone doesn't resolve. One example is a proxy that the PAC script names as `proxy-server`. A name with a dot in it is looked up as written.
* **Rules that test the device's address.** Inside the sandbox, `myIpAddress()` returns the sandbox's internal address, not the device's, so a script that chooses a proxy by client subnet can give the shell a different answer than it gives the device.

## Pin a proxy from managed configuration

> [!NOTE]
>
> Pinning requires Claude Desktop 1.44121.1 or later. Earlier releases ignore the `egressProxyUrl` and `egressProxyPacUrl` keys and keep following the OS proxy settings.

If you want the app, the agent, and (on macOS and Windows) Cowork's sandboxed shell to use a specific proxy regardless of what the device's OS settings say, set one of two managed configuration keys:

| Key | Value | Effect |
| - | - | - |
| `egressProxyUrl` | An `http://` or `https://` proxy URL, for example `http://proxy.example.com:8080` | The app sends its traffic through this proxy, and the agent receives it as `HTTPS_PROXY` and `HTTP_PROXY` in every session on the device. On macOS and Windows, commands in Cowork's sandboxed shell receive the same variables. Loopback and `.local` hosts still connect directly. |
| `egressProxyPacUrl` | An `http://` or `https://` URL to a PAC script, for example `http://wpad.example.com/proxy.pac` | The app evaluates the script per request. The agent receives the single proxy the script returns for your inference endpoint. On macOS and Windows, Cowork's sandboxed shell is handed a copy of the script when the sandbox starts and evaluates it per request itself. If both keys are set, this one wins. |

Both keys are read once at launch; a change takes effect the next time the app starts. While either key is set, the OS proxy settings are ignored for the app, the agent, and (on macOS and Windows) Cowork's sandboxed shell. SOCKS URLs and URLs with embedded credentials (`user:password@`) are rejected.

If you point the key at a local forwarding proxy on the device, give it as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`. An `https://` loopback proxy cannot pass TLS verification from inside Cowork's sandboxed shell, so the shell's commands fail to connect. The app logs a warning at sandbox start when it sees that combination.

These keys are read from an MDM profile, registry policy, or local configuration file only; they are ignored if returned from a bootstrap server. They also follow the same precedence rule as the update keys: when an MDM profile or registry policy sets any key in that group, values for these keys in a local configuration file are ignored. See [Update keys and managed precedence](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm#update-keys-and-managed-precedence).

On Linux, or wherever you deploy the local configuration file, the key sits alongside your other settings:

```json /etc/claude-desktop/managed-settings.json theme={null}
{
  "egressProxyUrl": "http://proxy.example.com:8080"
}
```

In a macOS configuration profile the same key is a `<key>egressProxyUrl</key><string>http://proxy.example.com:8080</string>` pair in the `com.anthropic.claudefordesktop` payload. On Windows it is a `REG_SZ` value named `egressProxyUrl` under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude`, or under `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude` if the rest of your registry policy is there. The app [ignores `HKCU` policy when machine policy is present](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm#4-deploy-the-configuration). See [Value types](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration-format#value-types) and [Deploy with MDM](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm) for the surrounding profile and registry structure.

Three behaviors to plan for:

* If the pinned proxy is unreachable, requests fail. The app does not fall back to a direct connection.
* If a pinned PAC script cannot be downloaded, the app connects directly and the agent gets no proxy. Cowork's sandboxed shell gets its own copy of the script through a separate download when the sandbox starts. If that download fails or returns something other than a PAC script, such as a sign-in page, the shell connects directly. The download isn't tried again until the sandbox next starts, so quit and reopen Claude Desktop on the affected device once the script is reachable. Combine the key with network-layer egress rules if a silent fallback to direct is not acceptable (see the warning below).
* Inside Cowork's sandboxed shell, a pinned PAC script's `myIpAddress()` returns the sandbox's internal address rather than the device's, so a script that chooses a proxy by client subnet can give the shell a different answer than it gives the device.

## What is and is not routed

The table summarizes which proxy source each kind of traffic follows. "App proxy" means the pinned key if one is set, otherwise the OS settings, with PAC rules applied per request.

| Traffic | Proxy it follows |
| - | - |
| App window, in-app sign-in, connection test, model list | App proxy |
| Inference requests from Chat, Cowork, and Code sessions | The single proxy resolved for the inference endpoint (from the pinned key or the OS), or Claude Code managed settings if deployed |
| Agent web fetch, plugin installs, and the agent's own remote MCP connections in Code sessions | Same single proxy as inference |
| The agent's remote MCP connections in Chat and Cowork sessions, to servers that a marketplace plugin or a user-added plugin bundles | Same single proxy as inference |
| Web Fetch in Chat and Cowork sessions, and remote managed MCP servers | App proxy (the app makes these connections) |
| Local (`stdio`) servers in [`managedMcpServers`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#managedmcpservers) | The app gives the server no proxy variables. Set `HTTPS_PROXY` in the entry's `env`, or have its `envHelper` script print it. In the admin console, use the **Environment helper script** field. |
| Sync of the plugin marketplaces you configure, and `aws` CLI calls the app makes for Bedrock sign-in | App proxy, resolved for the specific host |
| The built-in [GitHub connector](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/connectors-github#local-connector)'s calls to GitHub | App proxy, resolved for the host that serves the GitHub API (`api.github.com`, `api.<tenant>.ghe.com` for a tenant on `ghe.com`, or your GitHub Enterprise Server instance's own host) when the app starts the connector's server, such as at launch or after a sign-in. If the answer names only SOCKS proxies, the server connects directly. |
| Cowork sandbox download from `downloads.claude.ai` | App proxy |
| Telemetry and crash reports to Anthropic, if enabled | App proxy |
| OpenTelemetry export to your collector | App proxy for the app's own events; the same single proxy as inference for Claude Code metrics and logs |
| Commands in Cowork's sandboxed shell on macOS and Windows | The pinned key if one is set (a pinned PAC script is evaluated per request inside the sandbox), otherwise the OS proxy settings |
| Commands in Cowork's sandboxed shell on Linux | None; commands connect directly |
| The agent in an [SSH remote Code session](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions) | None from the device; the remote host's own network route applies |
| App update check and download | OS proxy settings only |
| Credential helper and header helper scripts you configure | None injected; the script's own environment applies |
| Brokered Microsoft Entra sign-in (Company Portal on macOS, Web Account Manager on Windows) | The OS broker's own settings |
| Pages opened in the system browser | The browser's own settings |

## Traffic that bypasses the app proxy

Some traffic doesn't follow the pinned key or the proxy the app resolved, or follows them only in some cases.

* **App updates.** Checking for and downloading Claude Desktop updates is handled by the OS-native updater on macOS and Windows, which follows the OS proxy settings only. This is the one app-controlled path with no admin-side option other than the OS proxy: neither the pinned key nor Claude Code managed settings reach it. If updates must not traverse a direct path, configure the OS proxy on the device or distribute updates yourself with [`disableAutoUpdates`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration) and your software-distribution tool. On Linux, updates come from your package manager, which has its own proxy configuration.
* **Commands in Cowork's sandboxed shell.** No proxy settings reach the Cowork sandbox on Linux, so `curl`, `pip`, `npm`, `git`, and anything else the agent runs there connect directly. On macOS and Windows those commands follow the pinned key, or the OS proxy settings when no key is set. When the key or the OS settings name a PAC script, the commands follow it only while the sandbox has [its copy of the script](#pac-script-for-the-sandboxed-shell). If the download of a pinned PAC script fails when the sandbox starts, the commands connect directly until the sandbox next starts. On every platform, [`coworkEgressAllowedHosts`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/web-tools) still applies inside the sandbox and sits in front of any proxy.
* **SOCKS proxies in Cowork's sandboxed shell.** On macOS and Windows, the sandboxed shell skips SOCKS proxies. Its commands connect directly to a host for which a PAC script returns only SOCKS proxies, and to every host when the OS proxy settings name only a SOCKS proxy. Have the script return a `PROXY` or `HTTPS` entry for each host that must go through a proxy, or [pin a proxy from managed configuration](#pin-a-proxy-from-managed-configuration).
* **Cowork's sandboxed shell when every host is allowed.** With a list of hosts in [`coworkEgressAllowedHosts`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/web-tools), the shell's commands reach the network only through a filter inside the sandbox, and a program that ignores proxy variables has no route around it. When the list contains `*`, that filter is off and commands make their own connections. On macOS and Windows they get the proxy setting only as `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY`, so a program that ignores those variables connects directly.
* **SSH remote Code sessions.** When a user runs a Code session on another machine through [`sshHostAllowlist`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions), the agent runs on that host and connects to the inference endpoint from there. Claude Desktop passes the endpoint address to the remote agent but not the pinned key, the device's OS proxy settings, or proxy variables from Claude Code managed settings on the device. The host's own network route and any Claude Code managed settings installed on the host apply instead. See [Inference credentials on the remote host](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions#inference-credentials-on-the-remote-host).
* **Pages opened in the system browser.** Some sign-in flows open your default browser. That traffic follows the browser's proxy settings, which normally track the OS; pin it with the browser's own policy (for example, the Chrome or Edge `ProxySettings` policy) or the device's network profile.
* **Brokered Microsoft Entra sign-in.** When [brokered authentication](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/entra-broker) is in use, the token request is made by Company Portal (macOS) or Web Account Manager (Windows), not by the app. Those components follow the OS proxy settings; configure them through the same MDM that manages the device.
* **Helper scripts.** An `inferenceCredentialHelper` or MCP `headersHelper` script runs with the app's environment and no injected proxy variables. If a helper needs a proxy, set it inside the script.
* **Programs that ignore proxy variables.** The agent passes `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, and `NO_PROXY` to the programs it launches on the device, but a program that does not honor those variables connects directly if the network allows it. The only complete control for this case is blocking direct egress at the network layer.

> [!WARNING]
>
> A proxy setting is routing, not enforcement. Nothing on this page prevents a process on the device from connecting directly if the network permits it. If you need a guarantee that traffic leaves only through your proxy, block direct egress at the firewall or secure web gateway and allow only the proxy. The inverse also holds: on an open network, a misconfigured or unreachable PAC script can quietly result in direct connections.

### The agent uses one proxy

The agent sends all of its own traffic (inference, its remote MCP connections, and in Code sessions its web fetches and plugin installs) through the one proxy resolved for your inference endpoint. Per-host PAC rules are not re-evaluated inside the agent. For most organizations this is the desirable outcome: everything the agent does is logged and inspected at one place, with nothing further to configure.

It needs attention only when that one proxy is not right for everything the agent reaches: typically some hosts (an internal MCP server, a private package registry, a self-hosted plugin marketplace) must be reached directly while the proxy only carries public traffic, or the reverse. In order of preference:

1. Let the proxy these devices use carry both kinds of traffic. Nothing else needs configuring.
2. Otherwise, list the domains that must connect directly in `NO_PROXY` through Claude Code managed settings (see the next section), using leading-dot suffixes such as `.example.corp`, and accept that everything not listed goes to the proxy.

The inverse edge case: if your PAC script returns `DIRECT` for the inference endpoint (common when the gateway is on your internal network), the agent gets no proxy at all, even for hosts the script would proxy. If the agent's other traffic must go through a proxy in that layout, set `HTTPS_PROXY` and a `NO_PROXY` entry for the gateway's domain through Claude Code managed settings.

## Interaction with Claude Code managed settings

> [!NOTE]
>
> The precedence described here requires Claude Desktop 1.44121.1 or later, the same release as the pinned-proxy keys above.

In Claude Code [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-files) on the device (a `managed-settings.json` file or an OS-level Claude Code policy), you can set `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, or `NO_PROXY` in the `env` block. Those values apply to the agent in Chat, Cowork, and Code sessions and take precedence over what the app would have supplied. Precedence is per variable:

* A managed `HTTPS_PROXY` replaces the app's proxy, and the app's loopback `NO_PROXY` entries stay in place.
* A managed `NO_PROXY` replaces the app's list. When the app is also supplying the proxy, the loopback entries are appended.

See Claude Code's [network configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/network-config) page for the variables themselves.

```json managed-settings.json theme={null}
{
  "env": {
    "HTTPS_PROXY": "http://proxy.example.com:8080",
    "NO_PROXY": "localhost,127.0.0.1,::1,.example.corp"
  },
  "parentSettingsBehavior": "merge"
}
```

Set `parentSettingsBehavior` to `"merge"` whenever you deploy a Claude Code managed-settings file alongside Claude Desktop on 3P, even if the file only sets proxy variables. Without `"merge"`, that file makes Claude Code ignore Claude Desktop's policy (network and filesystem sandbox, allowed MCP servers), except in a Code session that gets [`code` settings from a Claude apps gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway-config#apply-code-settings-in-the-code-tab). [Claude Code in Claude Desktop on 3P](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#interaction-with-claude-code%E2%80%99s-own-managed-settings) explains both cases and the merge behavior.

`NO_PROXY` matching in the agent follows these rules:

* A bare hostname matches that host exactly. To cover a domain and its subdomains, use a leading dot: `.example.corp` matches `example.corp` and `api.example.corp`.
* IP addresses match literally. CIDR ranges such as `10.0.0.0/8` are not supported.
* `host:port` entries match that host on that port only.
* `*` disables the proxy entirely, and only when it is the whole value; it is not a wildcard inside a list.

These settings reach the agent process only. The app itself and Cowork's sandboxed shell keep the proxy behavior described above, and the other paths listed under [Traffic that bypasses the app proxy](#traffic-that-bypasses-the-app-proxy) are likewise unaffected by Claude Code managed settings.

## TLS-intercepting proxies

If your proxy performs TLS interception, it presents its own certificate authority. The app trusts the operating system's certificate store. On macOS, the app also configures the agent to trust the System keychain in addition to the bundled CA roots, so a corporate CA installed there normally works without extra setup. To clone a [git plugin marketplace](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions#plugin-marketplaces-admin), the app runs the device's `git`, which reads git's system-level configuration, not the user's own.

If inference or tool requests still fail certificate verification, the CA was likely added with policy-restricted trust: certificates installed via `security add-trusted-cert -p ssl …` are trusted by Safari and Chrome but are not picked up by the agent's keychain reader. Re-add the CA with full root trust (omit `-p`):

```bash theme={null}
sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
  -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain /path/to/corp-ca.pem
```

If the certificate is MDM-managed and you cannot change how it is installed, set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` as a fallback, then quit and relaunch Claude:

```bash theme={null}
security find-certificate -a -p /Library/Keychains/System.keychain > ~/corp-ca.pem
launchctl setenv NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS "$HOME/corp-ca.pem"
```

`launchctl setenv` makes the variable visible to apps launched from Finder or the Dock (shell-profile exports only reach terminal sessions). It applies until the next reboot; to make it permanent, run the command from a LaunchAgent at login.

## Troubleshoot

**"Can't reach" banner.** The app could not get a response from the inference host the banner names. Behind a proxy this usually means the proxy resolved for that host is unreachable, requires a sign-in the app cannot perform, or does not allow the host. Use **Copy report for IT** on the banner to capture the details, confirm the device's OS proxy settings (or the pinned key) point at a reachable HTTP proxy, and confirm the proxy allows the inference host listed in [Required egress paths](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/telemetry#required-egress-paths).

**Confirm which proxy is in effect.** Open `main.log` in the app's [logs directory](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/data-storage) and look for these lines:

* **Key pinned**: at startup, `[egress-proxy] pinned to fixed proxy at proxy.example.com:8080; OS proxy settings ignored` (or `pinned to PAC script at …`)
* **Proxy handed to the agent**: logged the first time and whenever it changes, for example `Resolved system proxy for Code sessions: http://proxy.example.com:8080`
* **Last proxy reused**: a `Keeping system proxy` line, when the OS answer was direct, SOCKS, or missing
* **SOCKS answer from the OS**: a `Skipping SOCKS proxy entry` line
* **Proxy variables from Claude Code managed settings**: a line that names the variables set or replaced, and the settings file they came from
* **Proxy handed to the built-in GitHub connector**: a `[github-mcp] bundled server connected` line that lists `HTTPS_PROXY` under `envKeys`

For Cowork's sandboxed shell, open `cowork_vm_node.log` in the same directory and look for these lines:

* **Key pinned when the sandbox starts**: `[VM:start] guest egress pinned to fixed proxy at …` (or `PAC script at …`)
* **Sandbox's copy of the script not downloaded**: `[VM:start] PAC fetch from … failed (…); guest connects directly`

**Agent connects directly while the app is proxied.** The OS or PAC answer for the inference endpoint was `DIRECT` or SOCKS-only. Adjust the PAC rule for the inference host, or pin `egressProxyUrl`.

**New sessions keep using a proxy after the device leaves its network.** Once the app has been given a proxy for the inference endpoint, it keeps handing that proxy to new sessions while the OS or PAC answer is a direct connection, a SOCKS proxy, or no answer. Quit and reopen Claude Desktop.

**The built-in GitHub connector's tools fail after the device changes networks.** The connector's server keeps the proxy that the app resolved when the server started. Quit and reopen Claude Desktop.

**Cowork's sandboxed shell has no proxy on macOS while the app is proxied.** Check the PAC address in the OS proxy settings. The sandboxed shell uses its own copy of the PAC script. macOS refuses the download of that copy from a plain `http://` address unless the host is one of the exceptions listed under [PAC script for the sandboxed shell](#pac-script-for-the-sandboxed-shell). The app's logs then record `PAC fetch from … refused: macOS requires https for this address (App Transport Security)`, which you can search for in the [logs directory](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/data-storage). Serve the script over `https://`.

**Web fetches or MCP connections fail in Code sessions but inference works.** Either the proxy resolved for the inference endpoint does not carry that traffic, or the answer for the inference endpoint was `DIRECT` and the agent has no proxy. See [The agent uses one proxy](#the-agent-uses-one-proxy).

**Certificate errors.** See [TLS-intercepting proxies](#tls-intercepting-proxies).

# Overview
Source: https://claude.com/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/overview

Run Claude Desktop against your own cloud inference provider

Claude Desktop on third-party (3P) is a deployment mode of Claude Desktop that routes all model inference through a provider you configure: Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, any compatible gateway you operate, or the Anthropic API directly. The app runs from a bundled local web application. Conversation history is stored on the user's device, and on the remote host for [SSH remote sessions](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions).

You get the full Claude Desktop experience (Chat, Cowork, and Code, including file creation, multi-step research, and sub-agent coordination) with inference and billing handled by the provider you choose. [Unified Claude](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/unified-claude) combines Chat and Cowork into one experience.

## Who it's for

Claude Desktop on 3P is designed for organizations whose security, regulatory, or contractual requirements prevent them from sending data through Anthropic's first-party products (claude.ai or the Claude API). Typical deployments include:

* **Highly regulated enterprises on 3P only:** organizations that use third-party inference for regulatory or security reasons
* **International enterprises with data residency requirements:** organizations that require in-region data residency and cannot send conversation data to the United States

How far a deployment is separated from Anthropic depends on the provider you choose. On Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Amazon Bedrock, the cloud provider processes conversation data in the region you select. On Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic operates the Claude models, and residency follows the Foundry deployment type. Review [Data handling by provider](#data-handling-by-provider) and [Data residency and international deployment](#data-residency-and-international-deployment) before choosing a provider.

If your organization can use Anthropic's first-party products directly, standard Claude Desktop with [Cowork](/docs/cowork/overview) on a Team or Enterprise plan is simpler to deploy and releases new features more quickly than Claude Desktop on 3P. Choose Claude Desktop on 3P when routing inference through Anthropic's API is not an option.

## Architecture

Claude Desktop on 3P keeps the standard feature set and relocates inference to the provider you configure.

| Component | Standard Claude Desktop | Claude Desktop on 3P |
| - | - | - |
| Model inference | Anthropic API | Your configured provider endpoint (Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, or gateway), or the Anthropic API |
| Web application | Loaded from claude.ai | Bundled inside the desktop app |
| User identity | Anthropic account | Local device identity only (Anthropic account when managed from the claude.ai admin console) |
| Conversation storage | Anthropic backend | Local disk on the user's machine, and the remote host for [SSH remote sessions](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions) |
| Code execution sandbox | Local VM | Local VM (identical) |
| Configuration | Admin console at claude.ai | OS-native configuration (MDM-managed or per-user), a bootstrap server, or the claude.ai admin console |

The desktop app detects 3P mode at launch from the configured inference provider. When a provider and its credentials are present, the sign-in screen offers the option to skip Anthropic authentication and start the app using your inference-provider configuration instead.

### Security posture

* **Conversation content goes only to your configured endpoint.** The app sends prompts, responses, files, and tool outputs only to your configured inference endpoint and stores them only on the local machine. If you enable [SSH remote sessions](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions), Claude Code runs those sessions on a remote host, which also receives that content, sends it to your endpoint, and stores it. What happens to that content at the endpoint depends on the provider, as described under [Data handling by provider](#data-handling-by-provider).
* **Sandboxed tool execution.** In Cowork, shell commands run in the hardened Cowork VM; file access is scoped to your allowed folders and web fetches to your egress allowlist. For Code sessions, see [Applied as managed policy](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#applied-as-managed-policy).
* **Auditable telemetry.** [Crash reports and product analytics](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/telemetry#telemetry-categories) are scrubbed of conversation and user data before being sent to Anthropic, and can be fully disabled via configuration keys. Independently, you can export session activity to your own OpenTelemetry collector. The export is metadata only by default, with prompt and tool content available as an explicit opt-in. If you turn on [skill scanning](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions#skill-scanning), the export also carries records of scan results. A record's summary can quote the skill.
* **Centrally managed.** Configuration is delivered through your existing MDM (Jamf, Intune, Workspace ONE, Group Policy), a [bootstrap server](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/bootstrap), or the [admin console](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console). End users can't edit a configuration that MDM delivers. They can leave it for standard Claude Desktop by signing in to claude.ai. On Claude Desktop 2.37337.0 or later, a user who signs in to any organization that uses the admin console can move the device to that organization's configuration. To prevent both, restrict the device to Claude Desktop on 3P in the MDM profile, as described under [Restrict a device to one deployment mode](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm#restrict-a-device-to-one-deployment-mode).

For a detailed treatment of the threat model, sandbox boundaries, and data flows, request access to the [Claude Cowork Desktop Security Architecture Overview](https://trust.anthropic.com/resources?s=2a7bbzo1lyymvdt551q7kl\&name=claude-cowork-desktop-security-architecture-overview) on Anthropic's Trust Center. For architecture, telemetry, and controls information specific to Claude Desktop on 3P, see the [Claude Desktop Security Overview (Third-party platforms)](https://trust.anthropic.com/resources?s=0c8rx4s7mm5ierz8ppetfs\&name=claude-cowork-security-overview-\(third-party-platforms\)) on the Trust Center.

## Data handling by provider

Once conversation content reaches your inference endpoint, how it is handled depends on the provider you configured.

For Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Amazon Bedrock, data handling is governed by [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/data-governance) and [Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/data-protection.html) respectively.

Microsoft Foundry offers Claude models in two hosting options, Hosted on Azure and Hosted on Anthropic, and you choose one when you configure the model deployment in Microsoft Foundry. Under both options, Anthropic operates the Claude models and handles conversation data as an independent processor for Microsoft. Your use of Claude through Microsoft Foundry is subject to Anthropic's data use terms.

Deployments hosted on Azure run inference in an Anthropic-operated service on Azure infrastructure, not in your Azure tenant, and prompts and completions remain within Azure. The only data the service sends out of Azure to Anthropic is usage metadata and any content that Anthropic's safety systems flag. Deployments hosted on Anthropic send prompts and completions to Anthropic's own infrastructure for inference. See [hosting options for Claude in Microsoft Foundry](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-microsoft-foundry#hosting-options) for details.

For the Anthropic API, Anthropic processes conversation data under your Anthropic agreement, as described on the [Claude API](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/claude-api) page. For an [LLM gateway](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/gateway) you operate, data handling depends on the upstream provider your gateway routes each request to.

## Data residency and international deployment

**Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Amazon Bedrock:** Inference requests go directly from the user's machine to the regional endpoint you configure. Conversation data goes only to that endpoint, to local disk, and optionally to your configured OpenTelemetry collector. Residency is determined by:

1. The cloud region you select for inference
2. The physical location of the user's device, where conversations are persisted
3. The physical location of any [SSH remote session](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions) host, which sends that session's inference requests and stores its conversation

For multi-region organizations, deploy distinct MDM configuration profiles per geography so each user population points at an in-region endpoint. Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Amazon Bedrock each offer Claude models in the EU, UK, and Asia/Pacific regions; consult your provider's model-availability documentation for the current list.

**Microsoft Foundry:** Residency is set by the [hosting option and deployment type](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-microsoft-foundry#hosting-options) you select when you deploy the model in Microsoft Foundry. Deployments hosted on Azure offer two deployment types: Global Standard, which may run inference in any available region, and US Data Zone Standard, which keeps inference within the United States. Deployments hosted on Anthropic offer Global Standard only. Conversation history is stored on the user's device, and on the remote host for [SSH remote sessions](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions). See [hosting options for Claude in Microsoft Foundry](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-microsoft-foundry#hosting-options) for details.

## Public sector and highly regulated environments

This section applies when using Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Amazon Bedrock.

Because inference runs in your cloud tenant, Claude Desktop on 3P operates inside whatever compliance boundary your provider and region give you. The desktop application itself contacts Anthropic-operated hosts only to download the VM workspace bundle and Claude CLI binary (always required), and for crash reporting, product analytics, non-essential services (connector favicons, artifact previews, and MCP Apps widgets), auto-updates, and the published model catalog that labels the model picker. Each of the latter five can be disabled independently via managed configuration.

With Anthropic-bound telemetry, non-essential services, updates, and the [model catalog fetch](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#modelcatalogenabled) all disabled, the only remaining Anthropic-operated egress is `downloads.claude.ai` for the VM workspace bundle and Claude CLI binary at session start. An app managed from the [Enterprise Admin Console](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console) still contacts `api.anthropic.com` at launch and at each configuration re-check, and `claude.ai` at sign-in. If Code sessions can use Web Fetch, also set [`skipWebFetchPreflight`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#skipwebfetchpreflight) to `true` (or add `WebFetch` to `disabledBuiltinTools`), because Claude Code in [Code](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code) sessions otherwise checks each fetched domain with `api.anthropic.com`. Beyond that, the compliance posture of your deployment is determined by your inference provider. See [Telemetry and egress](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/telemetry) for the full set of network paths and how to lock them down.

## HIPAA

For Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Amazon Bedrock, Claude Desktop on 3P does not send user data, prompts, or completions to Anthropic, so Anthropic does not interact with PHI a user may upload to Claude Desktop on 3P. Claude Desktop on 3P transmits that data only to your cloud service provider and to any remote MCP servers you choose to configure. For a HIPAA-compliant solution, ensure you have a BAA in place with your cloud service provider and review any MCP servers for HIPAA compliance before connecting them to Claude Desktop on 3P.

Anthropic's API accessed through Microsoft Foundry (Hosted on Anthropic or Hosted on Azure) is an Eligible Service, as long as you have the HIPAA configuration enabled. Either option requires a BAA with Anthropic. See our [Trust Center](https://trust.anthropic.com/resources?s=l1wrssd9hsbi4gak0tp5a6\&name=%5Banthropic%5D-hipaa-ready-offering-implementation-guide) for more detail on implementation.

# SSH remote sessions in Claude Desktop on 3P
Source: https://claude.com/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/ssh-remote-sessions

How Code sessions run on a remote host over SSH in Claude Desktop on 3P, the sshHostAllowlist key that enables them, which inference credentials work on a remote host, and what to check before turning them on

An SSH remote session is a [Code](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code) session whose Claude Code engine runs on another machine that the user reaches over SSH, while the session's interface stays in Claude Desktop on the user's device. Claude Desktop connects to the host, places the engine there, and starts the session with the inference credential and policy from your managed configuration. Users can work on code that lives on a development server, a build box, or a cloud workstation without copying it to their device. In Claude Desktop on third-party (3P), SSH remote sessions are off until you set the [`sshHostAllowlist`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#sshhostallowlist) key, because enabling them sends your inference credential to the hosts users connect to.

> [!NOTE]
>
> SSH remote sessions are in beta in Claude Desktop on 3P and require Claude Desktop 1.40609.0 or later. The in-app configuration window marks `sshHostAllowlist` with a **Beta** pill.

## How a remote session works

1. **Connect.** The user picks an SSH host from the environment picker in Code, or adds one by entering its address, port, and an identity file. Claude Desktop connects through the device's OpenSSH client, or in some cases through its built-in SSH client (see [Host requirements](#host-requirements)), applies the host's entry from the device's `~/.ssh/config` (see [SSH configuration on the device](#ssh-configuration-on-the-device)), and prompts in the app if the host asks for a password or a one-time code.
2. **Deploy.** Claude Desktop places a remote server and the Claude Code engine under `~/.claude/remote/` in the SSH user's home directory on the host ([Host requirements](#host-requirements) lists every path) and reuses them on later connections.
3. **Run.** The remote server starts the engine on the host with the inference credential and policy from your managed configuration. Every file read, edit, shell command, and git operation runs on the host, in the working directory the user chose there. Claude Desktop connects to [managed MCP servers](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions#managed-mcp-servers-admin) from the device and exposes them to the engine as tools.
4. **Stream.** Claude's responses and tool output stream back to Claude Desktop. Permission prompts appear in Claude Desktop, and the engine waits on the host until the user answers.

The engine keeps running on the host through a dropped SSH link, device sleep, or the user quitting Claude Desktop. It finishes the current turn, or stops at a permission prompt, then idles until the user reopens the session. While Claude Desktop is closed, no new turns run and the inference credential is not refreshed, so a turn that outlives the credential fails with an authentication error. A restart of the app for an update counts as a quit.

When the user reopens the session after a quit, Claude Desktop rejoins the engine or replaces it, unless it refuses to start the session:

* **Rejoins**: on a macOS or Linux device, Claude Desktop 2.42304.0 or later tries to rejoin an engine that 2.42304.0 or later started. On a Windows device, Claude Desktop 3.1623.0 or later tries to rejoin an engine that 3.1623.0 or later started. If it rejoins, a turn still running goes on. It can fail to rejoin, for example after some Claude Desktop updates or after a change to the managed configuration since the engine started.
* **Replaces**: if Claude Desktop doesn't rejoin the engine, for example because a version older than the minimums above started it, Claude Desktop ends the engine and starts a fresh one from the transcript stored on the host. A turn that finished while the app was closed is shown in full, and a turn that still runs is cut short. If the turn stays stopped, the user sends a message to continue it.

On a host that ends a user's processes at logout, the remote server and the engine end with the SSH connection that started them, so a turn in progress doesn't survive a disconnect. Linux hosts where systemd-logind's `KillUserProcesses` setting is `yes` and applies to the SSH user behave this way. To keep remote sessions running through a disconnect on such a host, ask the host's administrator to exempt the SSH user, for example by listing the user under `KillExcludeUsers` in the systemd-logind configuration.

An idle engine stays on the host, with the credential in its environment, until one of these happens:

* The user archives or deletes the session.
* The user reopens the session and Claude Desktop ends the engine to start a fresh one.
* The host restarts.
* After an update that includes a new remote server, Claude Desktop replaces the host's remote server at a later connection. This ends the engines under the old server. Claude Desktop can put the replacement off while it believes that work is running on that host.
* After an update that includes a newer Claude Code, the user sends a message in the session. Claude Desktop 4.29.0 or later can then replace the engine with the newer version, if the engine has reported that it has no background or scheduled work.
* On a Linux or macOS host, 30 days pass without a connection from Claude Desktop to the remote server. The remote server then stops and ends its engines. Requires Claude Desktop 1.52386.0 or later.
* Someone ends the engine's process on the host. To list or end the engines and the remote server yourself on a Linux or macOS host, see [Files and processes on the remote machine](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop#files-and-processes-on-the-remote-machine). There the engine is called Claude Code, and the remote server the helper.

While Claude Desktop is disconnected, the remote server keeps the most recent output of each running engine in a 16 MiB buffer. It drops older output, and the engine keeps running.

On a Linux or macOS host, if Claude Desktop stayed open, it rejoins the running engine when it reconnects after device sleep or a dropped SSH link. It catches up from the buffer, and loads the part of the conversation that the buffer has dropped from the transcript stored on the host. If it can't load all of it, the session shows "Some output produced while you were disconnected may be missing here."

Some tool calls wait for an answer from Claude Desktop, and fail while it is disconnected:

* **File tools under a folder restriction**: if you set [`allowedWorkspaceFolders`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#allowedworkspacefolders), Claude Desktop checks each file read, search, and edit before it happens. While Claude Desktop is disconnected, each of these calls waits up to 10 minutes and then fails.
* **Tools that your policy sets to ask**: if [`builtinToolPolicy`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#builtintoolpolicy) sets a bare tool name, such as `Bash`, to `ask`, Claude Desktop is consulted before each call to that tool. While Claude Desktop is disconnected, each call waits up to 10 minutes and then fails.
* **Tools from MCP servers that run on the device**: these include your managed MCP servers (see [Where MCP servers run in a remote session](#where-mcp-servers-run-in-a-remote-session)). While Claude Desktop is disconnected, each call to one of their tools fails after about 30 seconds. The 30-second limit requires Claude Desktop 2.2553.0 or later.

For a task that uses these tools, have the user keep the device awake and connected. For other limits, see [Limits while Desktop is disconnected](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop#limits-while-desktop-is-disconnected).

### Account that a remote session runs under

On a Linux or macOS host, the remote server and the engine run as the SSH user. Installing and starting them takes no `sudo`. The shell commands and [MCP servers](#where-mcp-servers-run-in-a-remote-session) that the engine starts there also start as the SSH user. Review the SSH user's rights on the host, `sudo` rules included, as you would for a person who runs commands there.

### Alert the user with hooks on the host

A [hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) is a command of yours that the engine runs on the host at a set point in a session. With hooks, the host can tell the user that a turn is waiting at a permission prompt, has finished, or has failed with an API error, including while Claude Desktop is disconnected. To set them up, add this `hooks` key to `~/.claude/settings.json` in the SSH user's home directory on the host before the user starts the session.

```json ~/.claude/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "hooks": {
    "Notification": [
      {
        "matcher": "permission_prompt",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/alert-user.sh" }]
      }
    ],
    "Stop": [
      { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/alert-user.sh" }] }
    ],
    "StopFailure": [
      { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/alert-user.sh" }] }
    ]
  }
}
```

Replace `/path/to/alert-user.sh` with a script that you write and place on the host, for example one that posts to a messaging service that the host can reach. The engine runs the script as the SSH user and passes it the event as JSON on standard input, with fields such as `hook_event_name`, `session_id`, and `cwd`. The `Stop` event also carries Claude's last message, so forward only the fields that the alert needs.

Have the script print nothing and exit with code 0, because a `Stop` hook's output and exit code can keep the turn going (see [Stop decision control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#stop-decision-control)). To confirm the setup, have the user start a remote session on the host and send a message. The script runs when Claude finishes responding.

The hooks run in these cases:

* **A permission prompt waits for the user's answer**: the [`Notification`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#notification) hook runs once the prompt has waited about six seconds
* **Claude finishes responding**: the [`Stop`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#stop) hook runs
* **An API error, such as an authentication error, ends the turn**: the [`StopFailure`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#stopfailure) hook runs in place of `Stop`

The `Notification` hook doesn't run for a tool call that is waiting for Claude Desktop's own check. That check comes before any permission prompt for the call. Calls that wait for that check include these:

* Each file read, search, and edit, if you set [`allowedWorkspaceFolders`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#allowedworkspacefolders)
* Each call to a tool that [`builtinToolPolicy`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#builtintoolpolicy) sets to `ask` by its bare name, such as `Bash`
* Each call to a tool from an MCP server that runs on the device

While Claude Desktop is disconnected, each of these calls waits and then fails, after up to 10 minutes for file tools and tools set to `ask` (for each limit, see [How a remote session works](#how-a-remote-session-works)). Claude receives the failure as the call's result, and a further call of the same kind waits again, which delays the `Stop` hook. For a task that makes these calls, have the user keep the device awake and connected.

To cover every user of a host, put the hooks in [Claude Code managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-files) on the host instead, which on a Linux host is the file `/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`. If the host already has Claude Code managed settings, add the hooks to those and leave [`parentSettingsBehavior`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#parentsettingsbehavior) as it is, set or unset. Changing it changes how those settings combine with the policy that Claude Desktop supplies. If the host has none yet, also set `parentSettingsBehavior` to `"merge"` in the managed settings that you create.

> [!WARNING]
>
> By default, Claude Code managed settings on the host replace the policy that Claude Desktop supplies, even if they hold only hooks (see [Managed configuration on the remote host](#managed-configuration-on-the-remote-host)). With `parentSettingsBehavior` set to `"merge"`, the policy that Claude Desktop supplies still applies, layered under the host's own policy.

### Where MCP servers run in a remote session

An MCP server in a remote session runs on the device or on the host, depending on how it was added.

* **[Managed MCP servers](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions#managed-mcp-servers-admin), and servers from plugins in the [`org-plugins` directory](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions#organization-plugins-admin)**: the device. Claude Desktop connects to the remote (HTTP or SSE) MCP servers and starts the local (stdio) ones on the device, and exposes them to the engine as tools.
* **Local servers that a user adds under Settings > Developer**: the host, not the device. Claude Desktop sends the host a server's command, its arguments, and only those of its environment variables whose names start with `MCP_` or are one of a few fixed logging and runtime names, such as `DEBUG` and `NODE_ENV`. A secret in an argument or in an `MCP_` variable reaches the host. On a Linux or macOS host, Claude Desktop leaves out a server whose command is a path under a macOS or Windows folder, such as `/Applications/` or `C:\`.
* **Servers bundled in any other plugin that Claude Desktop copies to the host**: the host. The engine starts the plugin's local servers there, and connects to its remote MCP servers from there.
* **Servers in Claude Code's own configuration on the host**: the host. The engine reads files such as `~/.claude.json` in the SSH user's home directory and a project's `.mcp.json`, and starts their local servers and connects to their remote MCP servers from there.

With the device's OpenSSH client, the user's first message can wait up to ten seconds, with the line `Setting up your MCP servers on <host>…` under it. This can happen after a session starts, and after a quit, once Claude Desktop rejoins the running engine. Claude Desktop is handing the engine the local servers that the user added under **Settings > Developer**. If the engine doesn't get them in time, the message goes anyway, and the conversation shows `This message went without your MCP servers. If you need them, send it again once they're connected.` If the task needs those servers, have the user wait until Claude finishes responding, then send the message again. Requires Claude Desktop 4.4212.0 or later.

[`isLocalDevMcpEnabled`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#islocaldevmcpenabled), `managedMcpServers`, `allowedPluginMcpServers`, and `deniedPluginMcpServers` decide which of these servers a remote session loads, as they do for a local Code session (see [Applied as managed policy](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#applied-as-managed-policy)). If the host has its own Claude Code managed settings, those take precedence over the Claude Code policy these keys produce (see [Managed configuration on the remote host](#managed-configuration-on-the-remote-host)).

## Enable SSH remote sessions

Set [`sshHostAllowlist`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#sshhostallowlist) in your managed configuration. It appears in the **Code surface** section of the [in-app configuration window](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/in-app-configuration) while Code is enabled.

| Value | Behavior |
| - | - |
| Unset | Off, unless a Claude Code managed-settings `sshHostAllowlist` on the device allows hosts (see [Interaction with Claude Code managed settings](#interaction-with-claude-code-managed-settings-on-the-device)) |
| `[]` | Off. Delivered by an administrator, `[]` also overrides a Claude Code managed-settings allowlist on the device |
| `["*"]` | Users can connect to any host |
| `["build01.corp.example.com", "*.dev.example.com"]` | Users can connect only to hosts that match an entry |

While SSH remote sessions are off, the environment picker shows local sessions only, and any attempt to connect to a saved host is refused.

Each entry is an exact hostname, an IP address, or a `*.` wildcard.

* `*.dev.example.com` matches `dev.example.com` and any subdomain of it at any depth.
* Matching is case-insensitive and ignores a `user@` prefix.
* An IP address entry matches only that address.
* Entries do not restrict the port.
* A value that is not an array of strings counts as `[]`.

Claude Desktop matches entries against the `HostName` that the device's `~/.ssh/config` gives for the entered host, or against the entered host itself when the configuration has no entry for it or can't be evaluated. An alias is allowed when it resolves to a listed host, whatever the alias is called, and is refused when it resolves to a host outside the list. In the allowlist, enter the hostnames that aliases resolve to.

A session's [jump hosts](#jump-hosts-and-the-allowlist) must match an entry too. The allowlist limits which hosts Claude Desktop connects to. It doesn't limit what the device can reach over SSH from a terminal. Use network controls for that, and for a hard boundary.

For example, this Linux managed-settings file turns the feature on for one domain:

```json /etc/claude-desktop/managed-settings.json theme={null}
{
  "sshHostAllowlist": ["*.dev.example.com"]
}
```

In a `.mobileconfig` or registry policy, write the array as a JSON string as described under [Value types](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration-format#value-types). In a [bootstrap](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/bootstrap) response, the key sits inside the `codeSurface` object.

### Jump hosts and the allowlist

Add each jump host, or bastion, that Claude Desktop checks to `sshHostAllowlist`, by the `HostName` that the device's `~/.ssh/config` gives for it. Add the jump hosts before devices update to Claude Desktop 3.1623.0 or later, or users can't connect through them. To hold updates until devices have the new allowlist, see [Auto-updates](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/telemetry#auto-updates).

> [!WARNING]
>
> The allowlist has one kind of entry, so users can also start a session on any host that you list, and that session receives your [inference credential](#inference-credentials-on-the-remote-host). List only jump hosts that you'd also let users run sessions on.

Claude Desktop checks jump hosts in the `ProxyJump` that the device's `~/.ssh/config` sets for the session's host, or in a `ProxyCommand` written as `ssh -W %h:%p <host>`. If one that it checks isn't on the allowlist when the app connects or reconnects a session, the connection fails. When the user starts a session or sends a message, they see [Your organization doesn't allow this SSH connection](#your-organization-doesn%E2%80%99t-allow-this-ssh-connection), and the card's details give that jump host's `HostName`.

Find the names to add in a terminal on a user's device. Skip `proxyjump` lines only on devices where the built-in client makes every connection, for example with `sshTransport` set to `builtin`. The built-in client [refuses every `ProxyJump`](#ssh-configuration-on-the-device), listed or not.

1. Run `ssh -G` with a host that users connect to, for example `ssh -G build01`. Look for a `proxyjump` line, or a `proxycommand` line written as `ssh -W %h:%p <host>`. The command still counts with any of `-l`, `-p`, `-J`, `-q`, `-v`, `-N`, `-T`, `-x`, or `-a`, and the hosts after `-J` are jump hosts too. If a `proxycommand` line runs a program other than `ssh`, add nothing for it.
2. Run `ssh -G` with each jump host on that line, without any `:port`, and note the `hostname` that it prints. If the output for the first jump host on that line has a line of either kind, repeat this step with it. Ignore such a line in a later jump host's output.
3. Add each hostname, or a wildcard that covers it, to the `sshHostAllowlist` that applies on the device. To tell which one applies, see [Interaction with Claude Code managed settings on the device](#interaction-with-claude-code-managed-settings-on-the-device). Then have users quit and reopen Claude Desktop, because an open app keeps the list from a [bootstrap server](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/bootstrap#availability) or the [admin console](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console#configuration-updates) until it restarts.

### Interaction with Claude Code managed settings on the device

Claude Code has its own `sshHostAllowlist` setting, which you can deploy on the device through a [Claude Code managed-settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-files) or OS policy. The app resolves the two sources in this order:

1. `sshHostAllowlist` from the Claude Desktop configuration, when that configuration is delivered by an administrator: through machine-scoped device management (`HKLM` policy on Windows, a configuration profile on macOS, `/etc/claude-desktop` on Linux), through the [Enterprise Admin Console](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console), or by a bootstrap server the app trusts (a `bootstrapUrl` set through device management or covered by `trustBootstrapDelivery`; see [Keys that require user consent](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/bootstrap#keys-that-require-user-consent)). User-scope registry policy (`HKCU`) counts as applied locally.
2. `sshHostAllowlist` from Claude Code's managed settings on the device.
3. `sshHostAllowlist` from a Claude Desktop configuration the user applied locally in the [in-app configuration window](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/in-app-configuration#apply-locally-or-export-for-a-fleet).
4. Off.

On devices where users applied the configuration locally, deploy `sshHostAllowlist` in Claude Code's managed settings. That restricts SSH without an MDM profile taking ownership of the whole configuration (see [Update keys and managed precedence](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm#update-keys-and-managed-precedence)).

To turn off Code sessions that run on the device, so that users work in SSH remote sessions, set [`disableDesktopLocalSessions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#disabledesktoplocalsessions) to `true` in a [Claude Code managed-settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings#settings-files) or OS policy on the device. Claude Desktop then refuses to start or resume a Code session that runs on the device. If the device already has Claude Code managed settings, add the key to those and leave `parentSettingsBehavior` as it is, set or unset. Changing it changes how those settings combine with the policy that Claude Desktop supplies. If the device has none yet, also set `parentSettingsBehavior` to `"merge"` in the managed settings that you create. Without `"merge"`, the new managed settings replace the policy that Claude Desktop supplies to Claude Code on the device (see [Interaction with Claude Code's own managed settings](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#interaction-with-claude-code%E2%80%99s-own-managed-settings) on the Code page).

Before you deploy `disableDesktopLocalSessions`, make sure that the `sshHostAllowlist` that applies on the device, by [the order of its sources](#interaction-with-claude-code-managed-settings-on-the-device), allows the hosts that users need. While SSH remote sessions are off, a device that has `disableDesktopLocalSessions` set can start neither a local Code session nor an SSH remote session.

### Devices that move to an admin console organization

A device that gets its SSH keys from a managed profile, a registry policy, or the profile's bootstrap server moves to the configuration from the [Enterprise Admin Console](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console) when its user signs in to an organization that uses the console and chooses that organization in the dialog that follows. The app then restarts. A device that used such an organization before its profile arrived, and whose user hasn't signed out of the app since, moves back at its first launch on Claude Desktop 2.37337.0 or later, with no new sign-in and without asking the user, even if the stored sign-in has expired. To prevent that, add `disableDeploymentModeChooser` to the profile before devices update. `forceLoginOrgUUID` prevents it only for organizations it leaves out. Before Claude Desktop 2.37337.0, a device with such a profile ignores the admin console.

After the move, `sshHostAllowlist`, `sshTransport`, and `sshClientPath` from the profile, or from the profile's bootstrap server, don't apply, even where the console leaves them unset. For the profile's other settings, see [Which settings apply on a device with a managed profile](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console#which-settings-apply-on-a-device-with-a-managed-profile).

* **Which hosts**: the console's `sshHostAllowlist` applies. If the console leaves the key unset (**Not set**), or the app hasn't yet downloaded the console's configuration at this launch (the copy a device keeps of the last download holds no lists), `sshHostAllowlist` from Claude Code's managed settings on the device applies. With neither, SSH remote sessions are off.
* **Which SSH client**: the console's `sshTransport` and `sshClientPath` apply. On a Windows device, a client that the console's `sshClientPath` names makes the connection only if it is Microsoft's OpenSSH. With `system-openssh`, SSH connections fail under any other client. A key that the console leaves unset takes its default under [Host requirements](#host-requirements). Until the app has downloaded the console's configuration at a launch, both keys count as unset, so no client is pinned. Until then the built-in client makes the connection on a Windows device, even where the console sets `system-openssh`. The device's OpenSSH client makes it on a macOS or Linux device, even where the console sets `builtin`.

To prevent or limit the move, set one of these keys in the profile itself:

* **Keep the device on its profile**: set [`disableDeploymentModeChooser`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#disabledeploymentmodechooser) to `true`. The app ignores the admin console, and the sign-in screen doesn't offer **Or sign in with Claude.ai**. A device that has already moved returns to its profile at its next launch.
* **Allow only your organization**: set [`forceLoginOrgUUID`](/docs/cowork/hipaa-setup#what-each-claude-desktop-key-does) to your organization ID, and set the SSH keys you rely on in the console too. The key also limits standard Claude Desktop sign-in on the device to your organization. If users click **Sign in with Claude Console**, also add the ID of each Claude Console organization that you allow, as described under [Keep a device on its managed profile](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console#keep-a-device-on-its-managed-profile).

Before you add either key to a profile that sets only [app-behavior keys](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mdm#update-keys-and-managed-precedence), such as `disableAutoUpdates`, read the warning under [Keep a device on its managed profile](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/admin-console#keep-a-device-on-its-managed-profile).

## Inference credentials on the remote host

> [!WARNING]
>
> A remote session runs Claude Code on the SSH host with your organization's inference credential in its process environment, for as long as that process runs, including while Claude Desktop is closed. Anyone who can read that process's environment on the host, such as the same user account or a root user, can read the credential. List only hosts you trust with it, and prefer a credential that expires (single sign-on, or a credential helper that issues short-lived tokens) over a long-lived key.

The remote engine uses only the credential Claude Desktop passes in its environment. It ignores credentials already on the host, such as an AWS profile or application default credentials, and Claude Desktop copies no credential files there. Credential kinds that live in a file on the device are refused at session start.

| Provider | Works on a remote host | Refused at session start |
| - | - | - |
| [LLM gateway](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/gateway) | Static API key, single sign-on, credential helper | |
| [Claude API](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/claude-api) | Static API key, Sign in with Claude Console, credential helper | |
| [Microsoft Foundry](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/foundry) | API key, in-app Entra ID sign-in, credential helper | |
| [Amazon Bedrock](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/bedrock) | Bearer token, identity provider sign-in, credential helper | In-app AWS sign-in (IAM Identity Center), named profile |
| [Amazon Bedrock Mantle](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/mantle) | Bearer token, credential helper | |
| [Google Cloud's Agent Platform](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/vertex) | In-app Workforce Identity sign-in, credential helper | In-app Google sign-in, service-account key or credentials file, application default credentials on the device |

When the configured credential is a refused kind, the session fails at session start, with the card [SSH sessions can't use your model provider settings](#ssh-sessions-can%E2%80%99t-use-your-model-provider-settings).

When the remote engine's credential expires during a turn, Claude Desktop obtains a new one on the device, by re-running a [credential helper](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/credential-helper) or using a sign-in's refresh token, and sends it over the SSH connection. When the user signs out of the inference provider in the app, Claude Desktop ends the remote engine.

Where the host's [launcher](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#start-code-sessions-through-a-corporate-launcher) starts Claude Code, Claude Desktop passes no inference credential and refuses no credential kind. Claude Code uses the credential that the launcher or the SSH account's own environment sets, or, on Google Cloud's Agent Platform, the account's application default credentials.

The host needs its own network route to the inference endpoint and must trust the endpoint's certificate. Claude Desktop passes the endpoint address to the remote engine but not the device's proxy settings, CA certificates, or the user's shell variables such as `AWS_*` or `GOOGLE_*`. A gateway at `localhost` on the device is refused for remote sessions, because the host cannot reach it.

## Managed configuration on the remote host

Most of the policy that Claude Desktop applies to a local Code session applies on the remote host too. The [Code page](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#how-configuration-propagates) describes how each key reaches Claude Code.

* `disableEssentialTelemetry` and `disableNonessentialTelemetry`.
* `otlpEndpoint`, `otlpProtocol`, `otlpHeaders`, `otlpResourceAttributes`, and `otlpContentCapture`. Remote sessions appear in your collector under the same `service.name` as local Code sessions. A collector at `localhost` on the device is not forwarded. An `otlpHeadersHelper` runs on the device at session start, and the remote session keeps those headers for its lifetime.
* `disabledBuiltinTools`, `builtinToolPolicy`, `autoModeEnabled`, and `disableBypassPermissionsMode`.
* [`allowedWorkspaceFolders`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#allowedworkspacefolders), evaluated against the host's filesystem. `~` is the SSH user's home on the host, `%VAR%` entries are ignored, and Claude Desktop refuses to start a session in a directory outside every entry, so with a fleet value such as `~/Documents/Claude`, remote sessions start only under that path in the SSH user's home. For an entry with `mode` set to `ro`, see [Read-only folders on the remote host](#read-only-folders-on-the-remote-host).
* [`blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#blockreadsoutsideworkingdirectories), evaluated on the host, so the working directories and the home directory it hides from shell commands are the SSH user's there. Hiding files from shell commands needs the host's sandbox dependencies (next item); on a host without them, or a Windows host, shell reads outside the working directories ask for approval instead, and the file-tool restriction applies regardless. Files a user attaches to a remote session stay readable, except on a Windows host, where the session's plugin files and attachments stay outside the file tools' reach under this key.
* `coworkEgressAllowedHosts`, as Claude Code managed settings. The network and filesystem sandbox it produces with `allowedWorkspaceFolders` depends on the host having Claude Code's sandbox dependencies installed (see [Claude Code sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing)). Without them, commands run unsandboxed. See [Sandbox status on the remote host](#sandbox-status-on-the-remote-host) for the message the session shows.
* `managedMcpServers`, as the Claude Code managed setting that keeps the session from loading MCP servers that users define in Claude Code's own configuration on the host. The managed servers themselves are reached from the device (see [Where MCP servers run in a remote session](#where-mcp-servers-run-in-a-remote-session)).
* Plugins from your [allowed marketplaces](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/extensions), copied to the host. A plugin's `hooks` directory is not copied, so its hooks do not run in a remote session, and a plugin whose manifest declares hooks elsewhere is not copied at all.

If the host has its own Claude Code managed settings, those take precedence over the policy Claude Desktop supplies, as described under [Interaction with Claude Code's own managed settings](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#interaction-with-claude-code%E2%80%99s-own-managed-settings) for local sessions.

### Read-only folders on the remote host

On a Linux or macOS host, Claude Desktop applies `mode` set to `ro` on an [`allowedWorkspaceFolders`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#allowedworkspacefolders) entry by supplying Claude Code with permission rules that deny edits under the entry's path. The rules are Claude Code's own checks on what Claude does, not file permissions on the host. Where a folder must not change, use the host's file permissions to keep the SSH user from writing to it. Before Claude Desktop 2.31226.0, a folder with `mode` set to `ro` was allowed on the host but not read-only there.

A remote session doesn't enforce `mode` in these cases:

* **Windows hosts.**
* **Hosts with their own Claude Code managed settings**: Claude Code ignores the rules, and the sandbox settings that Claude Desktop supplies with them, unless those settings set `parentSettingsBehavior` to `"merge"`. Under `"merge"` the host's own values still win where the two differ, so `sandbox.enabled` set to `false` there leaves shell commands unsandboxed (see [Interaction with Claude Code's own managed settings](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#interaction-with-claude-code%E2%80%99s-own-managed-settings)).
* **An entry that is or contains the SSH user's `~/.claude` folder, such as `~`**: Claude Code keeps its own files there. List narrower folders.

Where the rules apply, they cover the following:

* **Claude's file tools**: they refuse to create or change a file under the path, even in bypass permissions mode. A writable entry listed inside a read-only one is read-only for them too.
* **Shell commands that Claude runs with its Bash tool**: Claude Code's sandbox keeps them from writing under the path on a host where it runs, which on Linux needs Claude Code's [sandbox dependencies](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing). The sandbox doesn't cover commands listed in Claude Code's `sandbox.excludedCommands`, or a path that contains one of `* ? [ ] ( ) { } | +` or a double quote. It may not stop commands in a folder that is listed through a symbolic link, so list each read-only folder by its real path, and keep it outside writable entries. On a host where the sandbox doesn't run, shell commands can still change the folder. For how the app reports that, see [Sandbox status on the remote host](#sandbox-status-on-the-remote-host).

The rules don't bind the SSH user, or other programs that run under that account. MCP servers on the host, hooks from Claude Code's configuration on the host, and the session's terminal (including commands that Claude runs there) can change the folder, and Claude Desktop and Claude Code can create git worktrees inside it.

### Sandbox status on the remote host

Claude Desktop asks Claude Code on the host whether the [sandbox](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#applied-as-managed-policy) from your Claude Desktop policy is turned on and running there. Requires Claude Desktop 2.26454.0 or later. If `coworkEgressAllowedHosts` contains `*` and `allowedWorkspaceFolders` is unset, your policy has no sandbox. For what Claude Desktop checks then, see [Sandbox from the host's managed settings](#sandbox-from-the-host%E2%80%99s-managed-settings). For a key that isn't set, see [Unset allowlist in Code sessions](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/web-tools#unset-allowlist-in-code-sessions).

The answer is Claude Code's own report, and Claude Desktop compares only part of it with your policy:

* **Folders**: Claude Desktop doesn't compare the folders that the sandbox allows with the folders in your policy.
* **Network hosts**: if the answer lists the network hosts that the sandbox allows, and a network host from your policy is missing from the list, Claude Desktop reports the reason `overridden`. Claude Desktop doesn't check for network hosts that the remote host's own settings add. Requires Claude Desktop 3.6556.1 or later.

When the sandbox isn't confirmed, the session continues and shell commands can run outside the sandbox. To keep Claude Code from starting on a host whose operating system has no sandbox or that lacks a dependency, set [`sandbox.failIfUnavailable`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#enforce-sandboxing-with-managed-settings) to `true` and [`parentSettingsBehavior`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/code#interaction-with-claude-code%E2%80%99s-own-managed-settings) to `"merge"` in the host's Claude Code managed settings. With `"merge"`, that setting applies together with your policy.

Find the message, or the `reason` your collector received, for the cause and the fix.

| Message in the session | `reason` your collector receives | Cause | Fix |
| - | - | - | - |
| Shell commands on `<host>` are running outside your organization's sandbox, which couldn't start | `cannot_start` | The sandbox is turned on but isn't running, for example because a Linux host lacks the sandbox dependencies | Install the [dependencies](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#set-up-linux-and-wsl2) on the host, then start a new session |
| Your organization's sandbox isn't running on `<host>`. Claude Code has no sandbox for that operating system | `unsupported` | The host runs an operating system that Claude Code reports no sandbox for, such as Windows | Use a macOS or Linux host |
| Your organization's sandbox policy isn't fully applied on `<host>`, so shell commands there may run outside it | `overridden` | Claude Code managed settings on the host replace your policy, even when they say nothing about the sandbox, or they turn the sandbox off or loosen it | Set `parentSettingsBehavior` to `"merge"` in the host's managed settings, and remove `sandbox` values there that conflict with your policy |
| No message | `unknown` | Claude Code gives no answer that Claude Desktop can read | In a session on that host, ask Claude to run the two commands under [Confirm commands run inside the sandbox](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#confirm-commands-run-inside-the-sandbox) |

> [!NOTE]
>
> On a device where the [local configuration file governs](#sandbox-from-the-host%E2%80%99s-managed-settings), Claude Desktop 4.16336.0 or later words these messages differently. They name `the sandbox from your inference configuration`, not your organization's sandbox or sandbox policy.

The fix for the `overridden` message and the fix for the message under [Policy status on the remote host](#policy-status-on-the-remote-host) start at the same setting, `parentSettingsBehavior`. With Claude Desktop 3.6556.1 or later, a session that shows one of the two messages doesn't add the other until the first no longer applies. Your collector still receives the event of the check whose message is held back, and the **Sandbox** row of `/status` still shows the sandbox's state.

To check one session, have the user open it, wait until Claude has finished replying, and enter `/status` in the message box. Where your policy includes the sandbox, the **Session info** card shows what Claude Desktop last learned in a **Sandbox** row. Requires Claude Desktop 2.31226.0 or later. Find the value's `reason` in the table of messages and reasons for the cause and the fix:

* **On · Strict**: no reason. Claude Code reports the sandbox from your policy turned on and running.
* **Off · can't start**: `cannot_start` or `unsupported`
* **Off**: `overridden`, and Claude Code reports no sandbox running
* **On · not fully applied**: `overridden`, and Claude Code reports a sandbox that Claude Desktop can't match to your policy
* **Couldn't check**: `unknown`

If your policy includes the sandbox and the card has no **Sandbox** row, have the user send a message, and enter `/status` again after Claude's reply.

With [`otlpEndpoint`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#otlpendpoint) set, your collector receives a `desktop_ssh_sandbox_check_failed` event under the `service.name` value `claude-desktop`, unless [`otlpDesktopLogLevel`](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/configuration#otlpdesktoploglevel) is `off`. A session can send the event more than once, for example when the reason changes or after Claude Desktop restarts, so count distinct `session_id` values rather than events. The event carries these attributes:

* **`reason`**: `cannot_start`, `unsupported`, `overridden`, or `unknown`
* **`sandbox_on`**: `false` when Claude Code reports no sandbox running, `true` when it reports one that Claude Desktop can't match to your policy, and absent when Claude Code doesn't say
* **`session_id`**: Claude Desktop's ID for the session
* **`backend_kind`**: `ssh`

The event doesn't name the host. To find the host, ask the user that the [user attribution](/docs/third-party/claude-desktop/telemetry#user-attribution) attributes identify.

### Sandbox from the host's managed settings

Where your policy has no sandbox, Claude Desktop 4.16336.0 or later asks Claude Code whether managed settings on the host turn a sandbox on, and reports one that isn't running.

Expect fewer reports than for a sandbox from your policy:

* **The session**: it continues, and shell commands run outside the sandbox. To keep Claude Code from starting instead, set [`sandbox.failIfUnavailable`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#enforce-sandboxing-with-managed-settings) to `true` in the same managed settings.
* **Reasons**: only `cannot_start` and `unsupported`, with the same messages, `/status` value, and event as under [Sandbox status on the remote host](#sandbox-status-on-the-remote-host). The table's rows for those two apply here too. Claude Desktop never reports `overridden` or `unknown` here.
* **A host that has the packages**: it can still report `cannot_start`, for example Ubuntu 24.04 or later without an AppArmor profile for bubblewrap. [Set up Linux and WSL2](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#set-up-linux-and-wsl2) covers the profile too.
* **`/status`**: the **Sandbox** row appears only after Claude Desktop has reported that sandbox as not running. After `cannot_start`, the row can stay for the rest of that session, so check a fix in a new session.
* **No report**: don't take it as proof that the sandbox runs. To confirm, have the user ask Claude to run the two commands under [Confirm commands run inside the sandbox](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing#confirm-commands-run-inside-the-sandbox).
* **The event**: it doesn't say which sandbox it is about. From a device whose policy has no sandbox, it is about the host's.
* **A device where the local configuration file governs**: Claude Desktop doesn't ask there. The file governs where neither device management, the Enterprise Admin Console, nor a bootstrap server delivers the configuration.
